author: brunorodolpho
body:
Three commits on dev `ceebab18`, all in test files.

## 1. The axis — the class #570's carriers cannot reach

#570's catalog-completeness guard has two carriers, both **reachability-based**: the composer fragment graph, and literal `resolvePrompt()` seams. Both enumerate what the runtime *wires*. That leaves one class structurally invisible to them:

> a persona that exists as an export but is **neither wired NOR catalogued**

An unwired persona reaches no `resolvePrompt` call and joins no fragment, so neither carrier can see it. It would sit in `personas.ts` looking authoritative while the operator surface has never heard of it.

The third carrier is #572's namespace walk — a thin caller, not a re-implementation. `personaExports()` rather than `promptTextExports()`, because the former applies that module's hand-written non-prompt exclusion. **This file carries no second exemption list**: `EXPRESS_INTENT_TOOL` filtering lives upstream and is proven live there by its own empty-the-list experiment; a duplicate would be a second place to drift.

Joins on **text**, not the export's name — the catalog stores `source:`, so text equality also catches a row pointing at the *wrong* constant, a prompt an operator could edit to no effect.

### Both arms, measured on the rebased tree, both restored by content

| Arm | Result |
|---|---|
| **1 — historical**: revert only #570's catalog row | 3 tests red, axis names `OPS_CLAIM_PLANNER_PERSONA`. Catalog restored to `07b384c4…` |
| **2 — plant**: add an unwired, uncatalogued persona export | axis reds **by name** while **all four #570 tests stay GREEN**. `personas.ts` restored to `a1880b67…`, marker absent repo-wide |

Arm 1 is a defect that really shipped rather than one constructed, and shows the axis would have caught F-67 independently. But **arm 1 alone would not justify the axis** — its class is one carrier B already covers. Arm 2 is what earns it.

## 2. The stale test name — declared drive-by, same class

`helpers/__tests__/prompt-surfaces.test.ts` had a case named *"personaExports covers the persona PROMPT_CATALOG omits"*. Measured **4/4 passing** — not a red; the assertion was always the durable one. Only the **name** stated a fact that expired when #570 catalogued the persona.

That is the same rot the last two PRs chased, one altitude further down: assertion (#573), file header (#573), now a test name. A name stating an expired fact sends the next reader hunting a defect that no longer exists. Renamed to state the durable property and cite no persona's catalog status. Flagged deliberately rather than folded in silently.

## 3. Carried strengthening from the closed #574 — credit to f63-worker

Its version asserts the union reaches **every** persona export rather than the one that happened to be missing. A single-name check survives none of add / retire / de-catalogue. Its rationale comment — the clearest statement that the original pinned the *defect* and inverted the moment the defect was fixed — is carried largely verbatim.

**Two deliberate departures, both measured:**

**(a) Anti-vacuity by non-emptiness, not by name.** #574 kept the single-name assertion below the loop, which does guard an empty walk — but it is a *name* pin, so retiring that persona would expire it. That is the same shape as the rule this pair of slices just established. `expect(personaExports().length).toBeGreaterThan(0)` buys the identical guarantee and cannot expire.

**(b) The comment now states what the case can and cannot catch.** `collectSurfaces()` builds its `persona:` entries **by iterating `personaExports()`**, so both sides of the comparison descend from one walk. I checked whether that made the assertion tautological. It does not — but it is narrower than it reads:

- **It is** a structural pin on `collectSurfaces()`'s composition. *Measured*: deleting the persona loop from it reds this case and the allowlist case. Restored by content.
- **It is not** independent evidence that the walk finds every persona. Nothing here could detect `personaExports()` itself under-reporting; that property belongs to the helper's own suite.

Naming that boundary is the point — otherwise the case gets cited as completeness proof it cannot supply, which is the overclaim this whole thread has been unwinding.

## Verification — re-run after rebase, not carried over

dev moved four times since I branched (#571, #572, #573, F-58 labels), so every number here is from the rebased tree:

- Neighbourhood — date guard, helper suite, prompts `__tests__`, `qa-prompts`, `ops-claims-plane-scope`: **8 files, 74 tests, all passing**.
- `apps/api` lint: **0 errors** (171 pre-existing `import/order` warnings, unchanged).
- Both #21 arms re-measured post-rebase and reproduced exactly.

Re-running the full neighbourhood rather than only the touched test is deliberate: assuming disjoint files means disjoint behaviour is precisely what produced the red #573 just fixed.

author: tharrosdev
body:
Phases 11 (NPC schedules), 10 (dialogue) and 9 (quests). **No defects found.** One cross-system rule surfaced that is the maintainer's decision rather than mine, so it is recorded rather than changed.

## Last hit wins — and a companion's hit isn't yours

XP, reputation and quest objectives all award on the same test:

```csharp
if (Entity == null || e.Killer == null || !ReferenceEquals(e.Killer, Entity)) return;
```

`ProgressionComponent`, `ReputationComponent` and `QuestLogComponent`, identically. So **a kill your companion lands grants the player nothing** — no experience, no standing shift, no progress on a kill objective.

I have left it exactly as it is, for three reasons:

1. **It is consistent across all three systems**, which reads as a deliberate rule rather than an oversight that happened to be made three times.
2. **Changing it is a balance decision**, not a correctness one — it has XP-economy and reputation-pacing consequences that are the maintainer's to weigh.
3. **It would have to move in all three at once**, or the systems would disagree about what a kill is.

Worth flagging because it *predates Phase 32*: the rule was written when nothing else fought for the player, and Kael arrived several phases later. The likely trigger is a play-through where Kael finishing a bounty target feels wrong. Recorded in the shortcut ledger with that trigger and the all-three-together constraint.

## Audited clean

- **`DialogueSession`** — the condition and effect tables are exhaustive, every *positive* condition fails closed and every *negative* one fails open (the correct polarity for each), and an unknown or empty `Goto` resolves to null and simply ends the conversation rather than stranding the player in a dead node.
- **`QuestLogComponent.Advance`** — snapshots the log before advancing, because a completion can chain another quest and mutate the collection mid-iteration. The guard is already there and its comment says why.
- **`ScheduleComponent`** — reaction states were read during the Phase 27 pass; the `_talking` freeze clears on any dialogue end, so a mismatched pair self-heals.
- Content integrity across dialogue graphs and quest targets is cross-referenced by `ContentValidator`, which reports green including graph reachability.

Gates: build 0 warnings 0 errors · 834/834 tests · `--validate` exit 0.

body:
"Restore WDK cache" costs ~293 s for a 1.8 GB cache while the driver build itself is 67 s — the dominant cost is per-file Defender scanning of ~50k small files during tar extraction. This adds a Defender path exclusion for the Windows Kits + VS MSBuild trees immediately before the restore in both workflows. If the image already has real-time protection off, it's a no-op and the unchanged step timing will tell us; next escalation if this disappoints is a single-file VHDX cache (mount + junctions), which eliminates the small-file extraction entirely.

**Hold merging until the in-flight attestation run completes** — touching driver-submission.yml retriggers it.

author: ashu11-a
body:
`branding/` held eight PNGs, a banner and a manifest describing where in a
Minecraft world they came from — everything except the thing that turns that
description back into an image. A new size, a different camera or a fix to one
material meant rebuilding the world first.

The scene is 2,069 faces of exported terrain across 25 block materials, the
four-part light rig, the portal's own light, and the orthographic camera at
41.9° elevation / 142.3° azimuth. Rendering it as saved reproduces
`logo-1024.png`.

Two things were wrong with the file as Blender left it, and both would have been
invisible until somebody opened it:

  * Its 33 textures were LINKED, at `build/logo/sweep/export/scene-03/tex/…` —
    a gitignored path that exists on exactly one machine. Anyone else opening it
    would have got an untextured cube. They are packed into the file now, which
    costs 47 KB.
  * It carried Blender's default 1920px / 4096 samples rather than the 2048px /
    512 the mark was rendered at, so pressing F12 would have produced something
    other than the committed icon. The saved settings are now the real ones.

`*.blend1` is ignored: Blender writes a rolling backup beside the file on every
save, and at 2.8 MB it is larger than the file it duplicates.

author: tiy1
body:
Audited every route across all 7 route files for RBAC middleware and audit-log coverage.

## RBAC

No gaps found. `requireAuth`/`requireRole`/`requireOrgRole` are applied consistently across every route that needs them.

## Audit logging -- five real gaps found and fixed

1. **Symptom log create/update/delete** had zero audit trail. Real health data -- matches the "who edited/who deleted" bar that exports and admin views already met. Added `SYMPTOM_LOG_CREATED`/`UPDATED`/`DELETED`.
2. **Cycle entry create/update/delete** had the same gap. Added `CYCLE_ENTRY_UPSERTED` (the create route is actually an upsert, and can't cheaply distinguish create-vs-update at the call site without an extra read) and `CYCLE_ENTRY_UPDATED`/`DELETED`.
3. **`DELETE /auth/sessions/:id`** (revoking one specific session) had no audit log, inconsistent with its siblings `LOGOUT` and `LOGOUT_ALL`, both of which are logged. Added `SESSION_REVOKED`.
4. **`GET /organizations`** (platform admin listing all orgs) had no audit log, inconsistent with `/admin/users` and `/admin/audit-logs`, which both already log `ADMIN_VIEWED_*`. Added `ADMIN_VIEWED_ORGANIZATIONS`.
5. **`GET /organizations/:organizationId/members`** (an ORG_ADMIN viewing the roster) had no audit log. Unlike a member reading their own data, this exposes other real members' identities (email, role) -- exactly the "who viewed" case an audit trail exists for. Added `ORG_MEMBERS_VIEWED`.

## Deliberately not added

Audit logging on GET/list of a user's own symptom logs, cycle entries, or trends. A user reading their own data on every page load isn't the "who accessed someone's record" case an audit trail is for, and logging every read would add a lot of volume for not much security value. The mutations are the actual signal.

## Testing

Added coverage across `auth.test.ts`, `symptom.test.ts`, `cycle.test.ts`, and `organization.test.ts` asserting each new audit action fires with the right actor/metadata. Also fixed `auth.test.ts`'s fixture ids to use `randomUUID()` instead of `"id-N"` strings -- the new session-revoke test is the first in that file to hit a route with `idParamSchema` validation, which requires a real UUID shape (same fix already applied in `symptom.test.ts`/`cycle.test.ts` for the same reason).

70 tests pass across the full affected suite. Lint and Prettier clean. Typecheck introduces no new errors versus the branch baseline (pre-existing errors are all from the missing generated Prisma client in this sandbox, unrelated to this change).

Base branch is `milestone-12-organizations` (same as the other open PRs on this milestone).

author: guarnz
body:
## What

Promotes the `stream` metadata (`stdout`/`stderr`) to an indexed label on collected logs.

## Why

Community Loki dashboards query with `stream=~".+"`, which requires the label to exist and be non-empty. Without it every panel returns `No data` — the query is valid and returns `status=200`, just with `returned_lines=0`, which makes it look like ingestion is broken when it is not.

Confirmed against the running Loki:

```
query="{namespace=~\"apps\", stream=~\".+\", container=~\"vaultwarden\"} |= \"\""
status=200 returned_lines=0 total_lines=0
```

`stage.labels` promotes the value the `loki.source.kubernetes` component already attaches, so `stdout` and `stderr` stay distinguishable — unlike `stage.static_labels`, which would pin every line to a single value.

Cardinality impact is nil: `stream` has exactly two possible values.

author: iderex
body:
Schließt / Closes #33
Schließt / Closes #35
Schließt / Closes #37

## Deutsch

Dieser Pull Request trägt drei Issues und nicht ein Thema. Das ist eine
Abweichung von Abschnitt 4 dieser CONTRIBUTING, und sie steht hier, statt
stillschweigend zu gelten. Der Grund: die drei schreiben je ein eigenes
Verzeichnis unter `presentations/` und teilen keine einzige Datei; jeder Commit
trägt genau ein Thema.

Zu drei Themen liegt jetzt ein Kapitel im Baum, und die `meta.yaml` jedes
dieser Themen beantwortet die Präsentationsfrage. Fünf dieser Antworten lauten
ja, und zu keiner davon lag ein Foliensatz vor. Ein Thema, dessen Antwort einen
Foliensatz verlangt und keinen trägt, sagt nichts darüber, ob jemand daran war.

### Die Dateien

Ein Commit je Issue, und jeder schreibt genau die Dateien, die sein Issue
freigibt.

`presentations/iso-iec-27001/management/` und `.../practitioners/`, je `de.qmd`
und `en.qmd`, für #33.

`presentations/iso-iec-27005/practitioners/`, `de.qmd` und `en.qmd`, für #35.

`presentations/iso-iec-27004/management/` und `.../practitioners/`, je `de.qmd`
und `en.qmd`, für #37.

Zehn Dateien in fünf Verzeichnissen. Dass es genau die fünf sind, die die
`meta.yaml` mit ja beantwortet hat, steht als Befehl unter Belege.

Zu einer Zielgruppe mit Nein entsteht kein Verzeichnis. Das Nein steht mit
seiner Begründung in der `meta.yaml`, und ein leeres Verzeichnis daneben würde
dieselbe Aussage ein zweites Mal machen und mit der Zeit von ihr abweichen.

### Entscheidungen, die der Plan offen lässt

Anhang A.8 sieht je Thema und Zielgruppe ein Issue vor, und #33 sagt, es werde
in je ein Issue pro Zielgruppe geteilt, sobald die Antwort vorliegt. Geteilt
wurde nicht. Die Fertig-Bedingung der drei Issues ist je Thema geschrieben und
verlangt einen eigenen Satz je bejahter Zielgruppe, und genau das liegt vor;
eine Teilung hätte fünf Issues erzeugt, die im selben Zug wieder geschlossen
worden wären. Wer die Teilung trotzdem will, hat sie noch: der Schnitt ist am
Verzeichnis vollzogen, nicht am Issue.

Der Satz für die Leitung und der für die Praxis teilen keine einzige Folie. Das
ist die Bedingung, die alle drei Issues eigens nennen, und sie ist nicht durch
Kürzen zu erfüllen. Sie ist hier so gelöst, dass die beiden verschiedene Fragen
beantworten: der Leitungssatz endet bei einer Entscheidung, die getroffen
werden muss, der Praxissatz bei einer Arbeitsreihenfolge. Zu ISO/IEC 27004
heißt das, dass der eine fragt, welche Kennzahlen überhaupt vorgelegt werden,
und der andere zeigt, wie eine gebaut wird.

Die Länge steht auf jeder ersten Folie und ist verschieden: 20 und 60 Minuten
zu ISO/IEC 27001, 45 zu ISO/IEC 27005, 15 und 45 zu ISO/IEC 27004. Eine gleiche
Länge wäre das erste Zeichen dafür, dass doch nur gekürzt wurde.

### Das Mittel

Quarto als Quelldatei, mit der Folientrennung über die Überschrift zweiter
Ebene, so wie das Muster in `presentations/de.md` es festlegt und wie der Plan
es entschieden hat. Es kommt keine Abhängigkeit hinzu, die der Baum nicht schon
trägt: die Quarto-Laufzeit steht seit dem Muster als bewusste Abhängigkeit
benannt, und eine `.qmd` bleibt ohne sie lesbarer Text.

Der YAML-Kopf trägt die sechs Felder aus Formatregel 3 und die Schlüssel, die
Quarto liest, in einem Block, so wie das Muster es beschreibt.

### Die inhaltliche Lesung

Sie hat durch einen zweiten Leser nicht stattgefunden. Für diesen Beitrag gibt
es keinen, und es steht kein Haken da, der etwas anderes behauptet.

An seiner Stelle steht, was geprüft wurde.

Dass zu jeder bejahten Zielgruppe genau ein Verzeichnis mit zwei Sprachen
liegt und zu keiner verneinten eines, ist gerechnet und nicht behauptet. Der
Befehl steht unter Belege.

Die Klauselnummern sind dieselben, die schon in den drei Kapiteln stehen, und
sie sind dort geprüft worden: gegen mehrere öffentliche Sekundärquellen, die
sich darin einig sind, am 06.08.2026, und nicht gegen eine lizenzierte Ausgabe.
Eine Nummer kommt hier hinzu, ISO/IEC 27001:2022, 7.1, auf der Folie zu den
Mitteln; sie ist auf demselben Weg geprüft.

Zu ISO/IEC 27005 und ISO/IEC 27004 wird keine Klauselnummer der jeweiligen Norm
genannt, wie in den Kapiteln entschieden. Beide Schlussfolien sagen, dass der
Katalogeintrag dieser beiden Normen `unconfirmed` trägt.

Die Zahlen im Beispiel zu ISO/IEC 27004 sind dieselben wie in der Anleitung des
Kapitels, damit ein Zuhörer, der danach das Kapitel aufschlägt, nicht zwei
Rechnungen nebeneinander findet. Sie sind erfunden, und die Folie sagt das.

Der Aufbau: jeder Satz nennt auf der ersten Folie Anlass, Zielgruppe, Dauer und
Voraussetzung, und jeder endet mit dem, was der Zuhörer danach entscheiden oder
tun soll. Jeder trägt eine Verweisfolie und eine Schlussfolie mit Lizenz und
Herkunft.

### Die Urheberrechtslesung

Sie hat durch einen zweiten Leser ebenfalls nicht stattgefunden, aus demselben
Grund. Die Fragen aus `copyright/checklist.de.md` sind hier beantwortet, und
diese Lesung ist bei einem Foliensatz die schärfere von beiden.

Punkt 1, Zitat: keins. Kein Satz aus einer Norm steht auf einer Folie.

Punkt 2, Aufbau des Originals: Hier liegt die Stelle, an der ein Foliensatz am
ehesten reißt, und sie ist beim Satz für die Praxis zu ISO/IEC 27001
beantwortet worden. Dieser Satz geht die Kapitel 4 bis 10 der Reihe nach durch,
und das ist die Nummernfolge und nicht der Aufbau: jede Folie sagt in einem
Halbsatz, womit sich das Kapitel befasst, und danach etwas Eigenes, nämlich
worauf man in der Praxis stößt. Der Gedankengang der Norm wird nicht
nachgezeichnet, und die Folie zur Reihenfolge, an der es hängt, folgt gar
keiner Klausel, sondern einer eigenen Beobachtung.

Punkt 3, übernommene Liste: keine. Die Maßnahmen des Anhangs sind nirgends
aufgezählt. Eine Maßnahmennummer kommt vor, 5.15, auf der Verweisfolie eines
einzigen Satzes.

Punkt 4, abgeschriebene Überschrift: keine. Die Folienüberschriften sind eigene
Formulierungen; keine trägt den Titel einer Klausel.

Punkt 5, Wortlaut: Jede Verweisfolie sagt, dass kein Normtext auf den Folien
steht und wo der Wortlaut nachzuschlagen ist.

Abschnitt 3 der Prüfliste, die beiden Stellen, an denen eigene Worte
umschlagen: hier ohne Gegenstand. Kein Glossar, keine Aufstellung über den
Anhang.

Abschnitt 4, Zuordnungen: hier ohne Gegenstand.

Abschnitt 5, die namentlich abgelehnten Fälle: Der Punkt zur Folie mit
Normtext ist der einzige, der in Reichweite kommt, und er trifft nicht zu.

### Die elf Formatregeln

Regel 1, Pfad und Name: eingehalten. Alle Verzeichnisse aus `a-z`, `0-9` und
Bindestrich.

Regel 2, Sprache am Ende: eingehalten, als `de.qmd` und `en.qmd` im
Zielgruppenverzeichnis.

Regel 3, YAML-Kopf: eingehalten für alle zehn Dateien. Der Befehl steht unter
Belege.

Regel 4, Verweise: hier ohne Gegenstand. Keine der zehn Dateien trägt einen
Verweis; wo eine Adresse vorkommt, steht sie in Rückwärtsstrichen als Text.
`scripts/check-links.py` weist über den Baum nichts zurück.

Regel 5, Querverweise auf Abschnittsnummern: hier ohne Gegenstand. Ein
Foliensatz hat keine nummerierten Abschnitte, und keine Folie verweist auf eine
andere.

Regel 6, CommonMark und Tabellen: eingehalten. Kein eingebettetes HTML. Die
Notizblöcke sind Quartos eigene Schreibweise und kein HTML, und die beiden
Tabellen sind Markdown-Tabellen.

Regel 7, Ansicht neben jeder CSV: hier ohne Gegenstand. Es entsteht keine CSV.

Regel 8, erzeugte Dateien: hier ohne Gegenstand. Es entsteht keine erzeugte
Datei; alle zehn sind Quelldateien und von Hand geschrieben. Was für eine
erzeugte Ausgabe gilt und wo die Regel dort nicht vollständig einzulösen ist,
steht in Abschnitt 5 von `presentations/de.md`.

Regel 9, Bilder als SVG: hier ohne Gegenstand. Keine Folie trägt ein Bild.

Regel 10, Festlegungen für CSV: hier ohne Gegenstand.

Regel 11, Unabhängigkeit vom Website-Generator: eingehalten, mit der
Einschränkung, die schon am Muster benannt ist. Die `.qmd` setzt Quarto voraus,
um vorgeführt zu werden, und der Plan hat dieses Format entschieden.

### Die Lizenz

Alle dre

author: jitokim
body:
## The incident

A `verify` node failed its check, and its reply held a precise diagnosis of what
had gone wrong — better than the operator's own hypothesis, and paid for at
**$1.36**. The engine kept one truncated `detail` line and threw the rest away.
The analysis was recovered by hand out of a session transcript that nothing in
the engine reads.

Then it happened a **second** time, to a node in this very lane, while the fix
for the first one was being built.

The failure class is not rare. Across 133 local runs there were 36 `node_failed`
events, of which 11 were `result_matches` misses carrying $21.33 of spend and no
reply at all — because for that class the detail is literally
`result did not match /<re>/`: zero bytes of what the node actually said.
`PersistOutput` ran only on `verdictErr == nil`, so on a failure the reply went
out of scope with the stack frame.

## The asymmetry that made it obvious

The engine already does exactly this for plans. A planner reply that validation
refuses is not discarded: `repair.go` hands the validator's refusals back for
one bounded, fenced re-plan, with the rejected call's cost disclosed.

|  | planner rejection | node failure |
|---|---|---|
| output | rejected spec kept (`PlanRejection.Spec`) | reply discarded |
| feedback | refusals **fenced** into one bounded re-plan | identical prompt re-run |
| cost disclosure | `PlanRepair.RejectedCostUSD` | a FAIL row, no artifact |

A node got nothing. `prepareRetry` changed two fields — it cleared
`ResumeSession` and minted a new `--session-id` — and the prompt, interpolated
once *outside* the attempt loop, went back out byte-identical. `resume
--retry-failed` re-ran the same prompt across a process boundary. The node did
not even know it had failed before, let alone what it had said.

## What is persisted, and where

`Handoff.PersistFailure` writes the reply to `<run-dir>/failed/<node-id>.out`
(atomic temp+rename, the same discipline `SetFeedback` uses — now shared rather
than hand-rolled twice; `OMG_HOME` still moves the base).

It is deliberately **not** `PersistOutput`. It registers neither an artifact path
nor a session, so `{{ artifacts.<id> }}` keeps failing for a failed node and a
`handoff: session` child still cannot resume one. Its own subdirectory keeps it
out of the flat artifact glob `docs/RUN-FEED.md` teaches, and away from a node
named `x.failed`. The directory now enters the RUN-FEED consumer contract, since
the read side has depended on it from the moment the reply became
machine-readable.

**The distinction the measurement surfaced.** The file records *"this node
ultimately failed"*, not *"this attempt failed"*. A retried node writes only its
final reply (`TestScheduler_RetriedNodeKeepsTheFinalReply`), and an execution
that PASSES removes the `failed/<node-id>.out` an earlier leg wrote
(`Handoff.DropFailure`) — otherwise the run directory would hold the losing reply
beside the winning artifact with a PASS in `state.json`, and `failed/` would stop
being a statement about anything. An intermediate attempt's reply still reaches
the next attempt's prompt; it just never reaches the run directory. The two
readers want different things: the retry wants the attempt it is repeating, the
human wants the reason the node ended up failed.

On top of that record, a retry now carries the attempt it is repeating (ADR
0016). The quote is the reply and **only** the reply — not the check's
expression, not its predicate name, not the detail that embeds them. Feeding
back a `result_matches` regex teaches the cheapest possible pass, which is to
print whatever it matches, and DESIGN.md already records a model writing
`**PASS**` and that exact reply failing a check. Withholding the predicate is
what makes gaming it impossible.

Only judgment failures quote anything (`isJudgmentFailure`, ADR 0010's split): a
spawn error, an interpolation error, `budget_exceeded` and a verification that
could not be *completed* rendered no verdict on the reply.

## The fence and the bound

The quote is untrusted model output entering a paid prompt, so it is fenced the
way every other such quote in this codebase is: a per-call `crypto/rand` nonce
carried in **both** markers, minted after the reply is already fixed so the reply
cannot contain it. `internal/coordinator/fence.go` moved to `internal/fence` and
is now shared — five call sites, one implementation, and the invariants guard
over that count reads the whole repo instead of one package. A nonce that cannot
be minted **drops the quote** and warns; it never degrades to fixed markers.

Two byte bounds, both cut head-and-tail on whole runes with the cut announced,
and both now pinned by their literals rather than derived from the constant under
test:

- **8000 bytes** in the prompt (~2k tokens). Exactly one prior attempt is
  carried, enforced structurally: `runNode` keeps `basePrompt` and every retry is
  rebuilt from it, so cost is flat in the attempt index rather than triangular.
- **256 KiB** on disk. There is no second copy of this text to fall back on, so
  an unbounded reply must not be able to grow the run directory without limit.

## The four proofs

One layer per package, all against `FakeRunner`/`FakeVerifier` — no real spawns.
Full suite green: 18 packages, `-race -count=1`.

1. **`internal/fence`** (8 tests) — the nonce is fresh per call, the excerpt keeps
   both ends and announces the cut honestly, and both cuts land on rune
   boundaries.
2. **`internal/handoff`** (15 tests) — the reply round-trips whole, registers
   nothing, bounds an unbounded reply, survives a dotted node id, does not
   collide with `feedback/`, and `TakePriorReply` hands it over exactly once.
3. **`internal/schedule`** (17 tests) — the reply is kept before `recordFail` so a
   consumer reacting to `node_failed` never beats the file to disk; losing the
   write does not change the verdict; the quote carries only the immediately
   preceding attempt, and a `run_error` actively **drops** a quote an earlier
   attempt was carrying.
4. **`cmd/oh-my-graph`** (2 new tests) — the cross-process case:
   `resume --retry-failed` re-reads `failed/<node-id>.out` for each node it
   clears. **This is why the reply had to be on disk rather than in memory.** The
   resume leg is a different process and it *drops* the FAIL record before it runs
   anything, so the file is the only account of the failed attempt that crosses
   the boundary.

The gate crosses with it as `runstate.NodeRecord.Judged` (additive, `omitempty`,
**no schema bump** — precedent `round` and `budget_usd`), read from the
unpartitioned snapshot because the record carrying it is one the retry leg drops.
Re-deriving "was this judged?" by parsing `Detail`'s prose would let a wording
change silently move a trust boundary, and without it a budget-killed node would
be told across the boundary that a check rejected it.

That cross-process leg is also where the last commit lands: it quotes into the
node's *first* execution of the leg, where nothing had yet cleared the session it
resumes — so a `handoff: session` node would have resumed its parent's
conversation while the quote appended to its prompt told it "You are a FRESH
claude session." Both halves now go through `startCold`.

## Costs, stated rather than hidden

This is **on by default** and it costs money: up to ~2k tokens per retry attempt
of a judged failure. Bounded and flat, never compounding. A knob defaulting off
would never reach a single graph anyone has already written.

Whether it raises retry pass rates is **unmeasured** — this repo has no harness
for that. The claim made is the narrower one: re-running a node with no knowledge
of its own rejected attempt is strictly less informed than re-running it with
one.

Named rather than left silent: `{{ feedback.<id> }}` still inlines a full model
reply into a body node's prompt with no fence and no length bound. That defect
predates this change; fencing it alters what body nodes are shown, which

author: marcelveldt
body:
# What does this implement/fix?

Playing a playlist on a group of Sonos speakers could stop after the first track: the track played to the end and everything went quiet instead of moving on.

A group player mirrors the playback state of its group leader, but the leader was the one player that never told the group anything. A player that has sync members of its own took the "notify my sync children" branch of the state fan-out and skipped notifying the group entirely, so the group only found out it was playing second-hand via one of the followers, or from its own 30 second idle poll.

Because the group still looked idle just after playback started, the queue skipped handing the next track to the speakers, and there was nothing to play when the first track ended.

Worth being explicit about the limit: the queue only tries this handover once, and gives up for good if the player is not reported as playing within five seconds. This PR makes the group learn its leader's state immediately rather than second-hand, which covers the normal case, but a speaker group that takes longer than that to settle can still miss the window. Making that handover retry is a separate change.

**Related issue (if applicable):**

- reported on Discord, no issue link

## Types of changes

- [x] Bugfix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue) — `bugfix`
- [ ] New feature (non-breaking change which adds functionality) — `new-feature`
- [ ] Enhancement to an existing feature — `enhancement`
- [ ] New music/player/metadata/plugin provider — `new-provider`
- [ ] Breaking change (fix or feature that would cause existing functionality to not work as expected) — `breaking-change`
- [ ] Refactor (no behaviour change) — `refactor`
- [ ] Documentation only — `documentation`
- [ ] Maintenance / chore — `maintenance`
- [ ] CI / workflow change — `ci`
- [ ] Dependencies bump — `dependencies`

Changes:

- Forward a member's state update to its group player(s) even when that member is a sync leader with members of its own
- Poll a Sonos S1 speaker again shortly after it reports a transitional state, rather than leaving it stale until the next regular poll
- Log why a next-track handover was skipped, so a silent stop is traceable

## Checklist

- [x] The code change is tested and works locally.
- [x] `pre-commit run --all-files` passes.
- [x] `pytest` passes, and tests have been added/updated under `tests/` where applicable.
- [ ] For changes to shared models, the companion PR in `music-assistant/models` is linked.
- [ ] For changes affecting the UI, the companion PR in `music-assistant/frontend` is linked.
- [x] I have read and complied with the project's [AI Policy](https://github.com/music-assistant/.github/blob/main/AI_POLICY.md) for any AI-assisted contributions.
- [ ] I have [raised a PR against the documentation repository](https://github.com/music-assistant/music-assistant.io/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) targeting the main or beta branch as appropriate.

author: jberdah
body:
Closes a loop: the bug CREATED the state that breaks entity routing.

## The collision guard checked only the canonical layout

If the target project held the same id in the pre-migration flat layout, the guard passed and the move wrote a canonical copy **beside** it — an intra-store duplicate id. That is exactly what the entity locator refuses as `ambiguous` (#177), so a *successful* `bclaw_move` could leave an entity permanently unroutable. Worse than the missed-overwrite the guard was written to prevent.

The source probe had the same defect mirrored: `resolveEntityDir(…, 0027read0027)` picks the canonical directory as soon as it holds any file, so a record still in the flat layout was reported "not found in source project" while sitting right there.

Both now use the shared `entityRecordPaths` primitive from io.ts — the fourth and last consumer of that export. The directory-vs-file confusion has one definition now instead of five look-alikes.

Found by a Fable audit, which ranked it the most serious of the remaining by-id sites.

## Verification

2 pins cover both faces: a legacy source is found and moved; a legacy record in the **target** refuses the move, asserting that a refusal leaves the source intact and creates no canonical copy.

Counter-proof: 10 pass → 8 pass / 2 fail, with the stash effect verified *before* concluding. Full default suite: 372 files, one FAIL in `review-loop-e2e` which passes 10/10 in isolation and passed in CI0027s full run for #179 on the same suite — cross-test interference in the sequential run, not this diff. Flagged rather than hidden. Lint and tsc clean.

author: thomaslevy-commits
body:
## Le défaut introduit par la #29

La [#29](https://github.com/thomaslevy-commits/site-internet-etude-notariale/pull/29) a ajouté des en-têtes de sécurité dans `next.config.ts` **sans voir que `vercel.json` en déclarait déjà une série complète, CSP comprise.** Le fichier existait avant, et le commentaire de `AccessMap` le mentionnait explicitement.

Deux politiques étaient donc envoyées. Quand un navigateur reçoit deux en-têtes `Content-Security-Policy`, il applique **leur intersection** — la plus restrictive des deux pour chaque directive :

```
vercel.json      connect-src 'self'
next.config.ts   connect-src 'self' https://va.vercel-scripts.com <endpoint formulaire>
                 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
effectif         connect-src 'self'
```

Conséquence : l'assouplissement introduit par la #29 était **sans effet**. Le formulaire de contact, une fois `NEXT_PUBLIC_CONTACT_ENDPOINT` renseigné, aurait été bloqué — et l'échec d'une requête `fetch` bloquée par CSP est silencieux pour le visiteur, qui voit son message partir sans qu'il arrive jamais.

## Pourquoi la CI ne l'a pas vu

Le job « Accessibilité et performances » sert le site avec `npm run start`, qui n'applique que les en-têtes de Next. **`vercel.json` n'existe qu'à l'exécution sur la plateforme.** Le job vert de la #29 validait donc une configuration qui n'est pas celle de production. L'affirmation « un job vert vaut validation », portée par cette PR, était trompeuse.

## Le correctif

`vercel.json` devient la **source unique**. C'est lui qui s'applique réellement en production et il couvre aussi les fichiers statiques servis hors routage Next.

`next.config.ts` revient à son état antérieur, augmenté d'un commentaire expliquant pourquoi les en-têtes n'y figurent pas — pour que la duplication ne soit pas réintroduite par mégarde.

Les apports de la #29 qui avaient une valeur propre sont portés dans `vercel.json` :

| Ajout | Effet |
|---|---|
| `frame-ancestors 'none'` | Interdit l'inclusion du site dans un cadre tiers (double `X-Frame-Options` pour les navigateurs récents) |
| `object-src 'none'` | Interdit les greffons obsolètes |
| `upgrade-insecure-requests` | Force les sous-ressources en HTTPS |
| `va.vercel-scripts.com` | Speed Insights, dépendance active du layout |
| `payment=()`, `usb=()` | Complète `Permissions-Policy` |

## Contrepartie assumée

`vercel.json` est du JSON statique : l'origine de l'endpoint du formulaire ne peut plus y être calculée automatiquement, comme le faisait la version TypeScript. `.env.example` porte désormais l'avertissement correspondant, au plus près de la variable concernée — c'est là qu'on le lira au moment utile.

La CSP de production n'est par ailleurs plus couverte par la CI. C'est le prix d'une source unique alignée sur la réalité du déploiement, plutôt que d'un test vert sur une configuration fictive.

## Vérification

`vercel.json` a été validé syntaxiquement et ses douze directives relues une à une. Node.js n'étant pas installé sur le poste de travail, aucun build local n'a pu être lancé.

**À contrôler après fusion**, sur le déploiement : que les en-têtes de réponse ne comportent qu'**une seule** ligne `Content-Security-Policy`.

author: brandonadamprice
body:
The high priest in the Tabernacle Explorer wore a breastpiece of twelve dots cycling through four colors (red, blue, green, purple), in a rectangle taller than it was wide. This makes the stones match Exodus 28.

## The twelve stones

Each stone is now the color of the gem named in Exodus 28:17–20 (ESV), in order, left to right and top to bottom:

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| sardius (carnelian red) | topaz (golden) | carbuncle (garnet) |
| emerald | sapphire (lapis blue) | diamond (clear white) |
| jacinth (amber) | agate (banded) | amethyst (purple) |
| beryl (sea-green) | onyx (black) | jasper (olive-green) |

Several of the Hebrew names are debated by scholars; these are the colors of the stones the English names denote, and a comment in the template says so.

## Also corrected

- **The breastpiece is square** — "a span shall be its length, and a span its breadth" (28:16). It was 12×15.
- **The stones sit in visible gold filigree** — "set in settings of gold filigree" (28:20). They were bare dots on a gold panel.
- **The two onyx shoulder stones** (28:9–12), engraved with six tribal names each, were missing entirely. Added to the ephod's shoulder pieces.
- **The ephod** now shows its skillfully woven band (28:8) rather than a single gold slab, and the gold plate on the turban is bound by a cord of blue (28:36–38).
- The figure is drawn about 40% larger so twelve distinct stones are actually distinguishable at the zoom the diagram flies to. It stays inside its existing hit area and badge, and reads proportionately against the bronze basin beside it.

The walk-through card for the high priest now names the four rows and the shoulder stones, so the text and the drawing agree.

## Testing

- Rendered the diagram in Chromium at the priest's zoom level, at the courtyard level, and fully zoomed out — no collisions with the basin, tent, or the numbered badge.
- Template parses under Jinja; `python -m unittest discover -s devotions/python/tests -t devotions/python` passes 117 tests (one pre-existing import error in `test_reminder_logic` from `pytz` not being installed in this container, unrelated to this change).
- Template-only change: no static asset `?v=` bump or `mobile/` version bump needed.

body:
This pull request introduces a new admin applicants management page, improves the admin dashboard UI and data accuracy, and adds a script for admin account creation. It also tightens security in user registration and enhances backend data queries for admins.

**Admin Applicants Management:**

* Added a new `AdminApplicants` page (`client/src/pages/AdminApplicants.jsx`) that allows admins to view, filter, and search applicants for each scholarship, with stage-based filtering and improved UI.
* Integrated the applicants management page into the app by adding a protected route at `/admin/scholarships/:id/applicants` and importing the new page in `App.jsx`. [[1]](diffhunk://#diff-51b002bf85fbd146b38871b89ba0d41c2bead37756295748c67206aac23ddc9aR11) [[2]](diffhunk://#diff-51b002bf85fbd146b38871b89ba0d41c2bead37756295748c67206aac23ddc9aR58-R65)

**Admin Dashboard Improvements:**

* Redesigned the admin dashboard UI (`client/src/pages/AdminDashboard.jsx`) with overview stats, improved scholarship listings, error/loading states, and direct links to manage applicants. [[1]](diffhunk://#diff-76ed5cd4078a52f4c234ecbf3958bfcd2e9e735241a46f9fa5cf19627fd2502aR6-R54) [[2]](diffhunk://#diff-76ed5cd4078a52f4c234ecbf3958bfcd2e9e735241a46f9fa5cf19627fd2502aL72-R253)

**Backend Enhancements:**

author: krelltunez
body:
## The bug

Deleting the iOS app does not clear dayGLANCE's data, and there was no in-app way to do it either.

The data lives in three places with different lifetimes:

| Store | Contents | Survives app deletion? |
|---|---|---|
| WKWebView default website data store (app sandbox) | localStorage, IndexedDB | No — iOS removes it |
| `iCloud.com.dayglance` ubiquity container | `Documents/dayglance-sync.json` | **Yes** |
| App Group `group.com.dayglance.app` | widget snapshot, share-extension queue | Derived, rewritten from state on next launch |

`WebView.swift` builds its `WKWebViewConfiguration` with the **default** data store — nothing is relocated into the App Group — so local web storage really is sandbox-scoped and really is deleted on uninstall.

The ubiquity container is the one that outlives the app. It sits at `~/Library/Mobile Documents/iCloud~com~dayglance/`, **outside the app sandbox**, so iOS does not remove it with the app. A fresh install finds an empty localStorage, reads the surviving file on its first sync cycle, merges it in, and every task is back — indistinguishable from the uninstall having done nothing.

**The invariant is about where the file lives, not about whether syncing is on.** The read is a local file read. It happens whether or not anything is reaching the network — which matters, because `ICloudBridge.isAvailable()` is a bare path lookup:

```swift
FileManager.default.url(forUbiquityContainerIdentifier: containerID) != nil
```

That answers "can I get a path", not "is iCloud enabled for this app". If iOS still vends the local container path when the user has turned the app's iCloud toggle off, `readSync()` finds the surviving file, `ubiquitousItemDownloadingStatus` reports `.current` (nothing to download — it's already local), and the app repopulates from a store the user believes they disabled.

There is a field report matching exactly that: iCloud off for dayGLANCE on two devices, app deleted, reinstalled, data back, sync confirmed inactive. **That specific mechanism is unverified on-device** and is recorded as such in the iOS doc, along with the check that settles it — a TestFlight/Debug build plus Safari Web Inspector, where `DayGlanceNative.iCloudAvailable()` returning `{"available":true}` with the toggle off is the confirmation. If it returns false and `localStorage.length` is non-zero on a fresh install, the surviving store is the website data store instead and the diagnosis needs revisiting.

Either way the reset below is the fix, because it deletes the file directly rather than going through a sync cycle.

## What changed

**`src/utils/resetAppData.js`** (new) — wipes localStorage, sessionStorage, every dayGLANCE IndexedDB database and Cache Storage, and at scope `'everywhere'` deletes the sync file via the existing `icloudFileTransport.deleteFile` (works on both the iOS bridge and macOS Electron).

- **The delete does not depend on syncing being enabled.** It's a file-bridge delete, so it removes the surviving local copy either way.
- **Cloud is deleted before local.** The reverse order leaves a window where the device is empty but the file is live, and a sync cycle in that window restores everything.
- **Nothing throws.** Each step records its own failure in `errors` and the rest still runs — a half-finished reset that stops on the first error is worse than one that clears what it can and reports the gap.
- **IndexedDB coverage** is the union of `indexedDB.databases()` and a hard-coded name list, since `databases()` is missing on older WebKit and the hard-coded list goes stale. Blocked deletes time out at 3 s rather than hanging the UI.
- **Scoped to dayGLANCE's own file.** `GLANCE/users/` and `GLANCE/events/` in the same container are shared with the other GLANCE apps and are left alone.

**Reset-in-progress guard** — checked by `useSaveOnChange` and `App.jsx` `iCloudSync`. During the wipe the React tree is still mounted and still holds every task in state; without the guard the next state change re-runs `saveData()` and the 15-second poll re-seeds the file we just deleted, both before the reload lands. Module-level rather than a ref because the writers live in different modules; cleared by the reload itself.

**`src/components/ResetAppDataSection.jsx`** (new) — open → choose scope → confirm, with the export-backup action adjacent. Wired into the mobile settings Backups view and the desktop backup menu.

The scope choice matters and the copy says so plainly:
- *This device only* — the copy in iCloud is kept, and this device can read it straight back **even if syncing is off**. For fixing a bad local state, not for starting over.
- *This device and iCloud* — deletes the file, so nothing restores it here or on a reinstall. Other devices syncing with the same iCloud account lose their data too.

The radio group is hidden entirely where there's no iCloud transport (Android, web, non-Mac Electron), and defaults to device-only so a mis-tap can't wipe a synced setup.

**Docs** — `docs/internal/dayglance-ios-app.md` now records the three stores and their lifetimes, the file-location-not-syncing invariant, the `isAvailable()` weakness as an open question, and the out-of-app equivalent (Settings → Apple ID → iCloud → Manage Account Storage → dayGLANCE → Delete Data).

## Follow-up not in this PR

If the on-device check confirms the probe is the weak link, `ICloudBridge.isAvailable()` needs tightening so the app doesn't silently read a container the user has switched off. That's a separate bug from the missing reset and is left for its own change.

## Also here: CI audit gate

Six advisories were published against transitive devDependencies since main last built, so the audit gate fails on main too — this branch's lockfile was byte-identical to it. Both have in-major fixes, so they're pinned rather than acknowledged, following the `brace-expansion` precedent:

- `fast-uri@3` → `^3.1.5` (via `electron-builder → ajv`)
- `undici@7` → `^7.29.0` (via `electron → @electron/get`)

Scoped per-major so `undici@6` under `node-gyp` is untouched — those advisories are `>=7.0.0` only. Both packages are build/dev-time and ship in no bundle. Kept as its own commit so it reviews separately.

## Testing

- `src/utils/resetAppData.test.js` (new, 22 cases) — all platform APIs injected, so no browser needed. Covers both scopes, the cloud-before-local ordering guarantee, per-step failure isolation, the blocked-delete timeout, the `databases()` union, and that the guard is raised before any wipe step runs.
- Full suite: 1156 tests / 78 files passing.
- `eslint --max-warnings 0` clean.
- Web and iOS bundles build.
- Not yet exercised on a physical iOS device.

author: julystar-lv
body:
## Summary

Adopt the recommended Halcyon-inspired Android media-control architecture while preserving MelodyTrove's explicit OEM media-key fallback and application-level queue semantics.

## Queue ownership

- publish a bounded 101-item window of the real application queue into the Media3 timeline
- keep the current item centered and rebuild the window near its edges
- synchronize queue reorder, requested-next changes, and queue edits back into Media3 while preserving the current position and play state
- include stable media IDs plus global queue index/count metadata
- avoid sending very large libraries or embedded artwork through Binder

## On-demand playback resources

- use lightweight `melodytrove://track/<id>` queue URIs
- resolve local, WebDAV, SMB, OneDrive, and cached resources only when Media3 opens an item
- forward source-specific request headers to the upstream data source
- enforce existing offline/metered-network policy and retry settings
- release temporary playback resources when the Media3 data source closes

## Playback state and controller semantics

- prefer native Media3 queue loading through the Android `MediaController`
- retain the previous single-item preparation path as a fallback for test/fake engines
- synchronize automatic Media3 transitions back to `PlayerRepository`
- update replay gain, metadata, artwork, duration, notification state, and the UI after external or automatic transitions
- use `ForwardingPlayer` so every explicit next/previous command delegates to the application controller, preserving true-random shuffle, requested-next ordering, repeat policy, and queue boundaries
- keep automatic transitions on the native Media3 timeline
- map external STOP to a resumable pause, while internal app stop explicitly clears the Media3 timeline

## Android Auto and media browsing

- convert `PlaybackService` to `MediaLibraryService`
- advertise both the Media3 library-service interface and the legacy platform media-browser interface
- expose a root node and a paginated, playable current-queue node
- hydrate Media1/legacy Android Auto playback requests by media ID
- notify subscribed browsers when the application queue changes

## Physical and OEM media controls

- retain explicit handling of play, pause, stop, next, previous, fast-forward, rewind, skip-forward, skip-backward, and headset-hook events
- continue consuming complete recognized key sequences to prevent duplicate Media3 actions
- route explicit next/previous keys through the same wrapped session-player semantics used by Android Auto, Bluetooth, Wear OS, and other controllers

## Validation

- Android debug APK build
- Desktop/shared Kotlin tests
- Rust checks
- complete iOS simulator application build (cross-platform regression check)

The Overview's upload-task table and the Queues **Depth** tab listed every `(kind, state)` pair with equal weight — which in practice means `DONE`. author: mrsirquanzo
body:
The README described the pre-redesign engine. Two things that now define Sonny were absent:

- **Modality-agnostic.** The rubric is fixed and deterministic; the resolved modality conditions it through a lens rather than rewriting it, and retrieval states facts without naming a modality — so a small-molecule run is not quietly told it is an antibody run.
- **Answerable about its gaps.** A dossier ships with the questions specialists could not answer, and an absence claim must be substantiated by retrieval audits showing the searches that actually ran.

`Status` claimed the roadmap was hardening "the multimodal and knowledge-graph layers", which is neither what was built nor what is next. Replaced with what is merged plus a pointer to `docs/slices/STATUS.md` for deferred work and the known evaluation-harness gaps, rather than restating a roadmap that will drift again.

Architecture entries now name the conclusion contracts, disease-context keys, risk taxonomy, retrieval audits, question ledger, and the investigation metrics.

Docs only. The repo description and topics were updated separately on GitHub.

💡 What: Replaced chained `.map()` and spread `Math.min/max()` calls with single pass `for...of` and `for` loops in `AssetsPanel.tsx`, `geometryOracle.ts`, and `rotation3d.ts`.
🎯 Why: Using the spread operator (`...`) on large arrays (especially when chained after a `.map()` allocation) causes redundant O(N) memory allocations, garbage collection pressure, and critically, `Maximum call stack size exceeded` errors if the dataset is too large.
📊 Impact: Eliminates array allocation overhead during bounding box and layout calculations, creating an O(N) performance win and preventing application crashes on large inputs.
🔬 Measurement: Verify tests continue to pass (`pnpm test tests/geometry/bounding.test.ts`), and memory usage profile during large rotations or group bounds rendering.

## What this fixes

The known-failure list was written from a run two days older than the branches merged on top of it, so seven of its entries recorded tests that had since been fixed.

A listed test that starts passing is itself a merge block — the rule exists so the list can't rot into a permanent excuse. Which meant the list was blocking on the very work that repaired it. My error: I built it from stale data because we didn't want to wait for a fresh run.

## Removed

| Entry | Fixed by |
|---|---|
| `biscuit-speaks/windows-latest/L1` | the cache-file race (#39) |
| `tree-hugger/windows-latest/L1` | portable paths in the hug CLI (#35) |

| `model-citizen/windows-latest/L1` | no longer failing |
| `schematic/wsl2-ubuntu/L1` | no longer failing |

39 → 32 entries. Nothing added, nothing reworded.

## Source

Main's own run [31041986681](https://github.com/yankeeinlondon/rusty-biscuit/actions/runs/31041986681) — the first full run after those merges, and the first with today's scoping changes in place.

**That run reports zero `cell-failed` blocks.** Every real test failure on main is now covered by the list, and the seven merges introduced nothing new. Its only blocks were the seven stale entries this PR removes, plus one more below.

## The one thing left

Re-running the verdict locally against this file leaves two blocks, both the same root cause:

```
BLOCK  baseline-no-result  unchained-ai/wsl2-ubuntu/L1 shard 1/1
BLOCK  cell-missing        unchained-ai/wsl2-ubuntu/L1
```

That leg produced no report at all because the WSL2 guest **failed to provision**:

```

the WSL2 guest failed to provision (attempt 1 …, attempt 2 …); no test could run
```

Infrastructure, not code — and not something the list can excuse, because a missing report blocks on its own regardless of any entry. Likely clears on a re-run; recorded here rather than papered over.

## Verified

author: apage224
body:
## Summary

Replace the post-release `refresh-uv-lock` follow-up PR (opened via `peter-evans/create-pull-request` on the long-lived `automation/update-uv-lock` branch, hand-editing `uv.lock`'s editable version line with a regex *after* publish) with a pre-merge sync: a new `sync-release-lock` job runs `uv lock` directly on the Release Please branch, right after that PR is created or updated, and pushes `uv.lock` back to the same branch if it changed. There is no follow-up PR anymore, and every release lands on `main` with `uv.lock` already in sync with `pyproject.toml`.

## What changed (`.github/workflows/release.yml`)

- **New `sync-release-lock` job** (needs `release-please`, runs only when a release PR exists):
  1. Validates the reported PR's head branch name against `release-please--branches--main--components--<package-name>` (derived from this repo's own `release-please-config.json`), then cross-checks via `gh api .../pulls/$number` that the PR is **open** and **entirely within this repository** (`head.repo.full_name`/`base.repo.full_name` both equal `$GITHUB_REPOSITORY` — never a fork or unrelated PR), and that `head.sha` is a full 40-hex commit SHA.
  2. Fetches and checks out that exact validated commit (re-verifying the fetched SHA before creating a local branch from it).
  3. Runs `uv lock` — the canonical resolver command, not a regex edit — so the editable `neuralspotx` version and any other lock metadata stay coherent with the bumped `pyproject.toml`.
  4. If `uv.lock` changed, commits **only** `uv.lock` (fails closed if any other file changed) as `github-actions[bot]` and does a plain, **non-force** `git push origin HEAD:refs/heads/$BRANCH` back to that branch. If the push is rejected (e.g. branch protection), falls back to a single-file commit via the GitHub Contents API — but only after re-confirming the remote branch head hasn't moved since validation.
  5. If `uv.lock` didn't change, it's a no-op that still reports the (unchanged) validated head SHA.

- **`dispatch-release-pr-ci`** now depends on `sync-release-lock` (previously depended directly on `release-please`), re-confirms the branch's *current* remote head matches the lock-sync job's recorded head, and only then dispatches CI. This guarantees the release PR's required status check always covers the final, lock-synced commit — never the pre-sync Release Please commit.

- **`release-metadata`**'s `release_created` detection no longer diffs `pyproject.toml` between `HEAD` and `HEAD^` on `main`. Now that the release PR can carry a second (lock-sync) commit, that comparison breaks under a **rebase merge** (still enabled on this repo — confirmed via `gh api repos/AmbiqAI/neuralspotx`, `allow_rebase_merge: true`): both commits would land on `main`, making `HEAD^` the version-bump commit and silently skipping tag creation, the GitHub release, and PyPI publish, with a green workflow. Detection is now based on whether the release tag already exists — merge-method- and commit-count-agnostic.

- **Repository-wide `concurrency`** (`group: release`, `cancel-in-progress: false`, **`queue: max`**) serializes all invocations of this workflow. `queue: max` specifically matters here: the default `queue: single` cancels an already-*pending* run the instant a second run queues behind it (per [GitHub's documented concurrency semantics](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/write-workflows/choose-when-workflows-run/control-workflow-concurrency)), which could silently drop a release-landing run waiting behind `exact-commit-ci`'s multi-minute poll.

- **Removed**: `refresh-uv-lock`, `dispatch-lock-refresh-ci`, the `peter-evans/create-pull-request` dependency, the `automation/update-uv-lock` branch, and the `pull-requests: write` permission that only those jobs needed.

- **Unchanged**: `release-context`/`exact-commit-ci`/`create-release-tag`/`build`/`github-release`/`pypi-publish` — the publisher still keys off `github.sha` (the merged release-landing commit on `main`), never the release-please branch or the lock-sync commit. Exact-commit CI, immutable annotated tag creation, and PyPI/GitHub publication are untouched.

## Docs

`docs/contributing/releases.md`: replaced the "uv.lock Refresh" section with "uv.lock Sync" describing the new pre-merge flow (including the branch-protection fallback and the merge-method-agnostic release detection), updated the mermaid diagram, and corrected/documented the `queue: max` concurrency behavior.

## Tests

`tests/test_release_workflow.py` grew from 4 to 19 static assertions over the workflow YAML/text, covering: job ordering (`sync-release-lock` between `release-please` and `dispatch-release-pr-ci`), canonical `uv lock` (no regex mutation), CI dispatch against the final synced head, idempotent no-change handling, only-`uv.lock`-committed enforcement, branch/PR validation, bot identity + non-force push (including a `+HEAD` force-refspec guard), the branch-protection fallback's re-validation (scoped to the `sync-release-lock` job's own raw source so it can't pass by coincidence via `dispatch-release-pr-ci`'s separate copy), a structural check that **every** `gh`-CLI-invoking step across the whole file declares `GH_TOKEN` in its own step env, removal of the old jobs/action/branch, the unchanged publish path, the `concurrency`/`queue: max` block, and no release-workflow loop.

I mutation-tested three of these (removing the fallback's re-validation, removing the push step's `GH_TOKEN`, and switching to a `+HEAD` force-push refspec) and confirmed each failure is caught.

## Validation

- `python -c "import yaml; yaml.safe_load(open('.github/workflows/release.yml'))"` — parses.
- `actionlint .github/workflows/release.yml` — no new findings beyond the pre-existing style-level shellcheck notes also present on `origin/main`; the tool doesn't yet recognize the `queue` concurrency key (open upstream issues [rhysd/actionlint#657](https://github.com/rhysd/actionlint/issues/657), [#680](https://github.com/rhysd/actionlint/issues/680)) even though it's a real, GA GitHub Actions feature ([docs](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/write-workflows/choose-when-workflows-run/control-workflow-concurrency), in production use in e.g. `ggml-org/llama.cpp`, `Azure/azure-sdk-for-net`).
- `uv run --group lint ruff check .` — all checks passed.
- `uv run --group test pytest -q` — 964 passed, 2 skipped (full suite; baseline before this change was 961 passed, 2 skipped).
- `uv lock --check` — in sync; `uv.lock` is untouched by this change.
- `uv run --group docs zensical build` — docs build clean, no warnings.

## Review

Independently reviewed by Opus 5 and Fable 5 (long-context, read-only code review). Both flagged the same three real issues, which are fixed in this PR:
1. The `Commit and push uv.lock` step's Contents-API fallback was missing `GH_TOKEN`, so it could never actually run.
2. `uv.lock` (~175 KB) base64-encodes to more than Linux's ~128 KiB single-argument limit, so the fallback's original `--field content=<b64>` would fail with "Argument list too long" even with a token — fixed by writing the payload to `$RUNNER_TEMP` and using `gh`'s `@file` field syntax.
3. `release-metadata`'s `HEAD`/`HEAD^` diff would silently skip a release under a rebase merge now that the branch can carry two commits — fixed by switching to tag-existence detection.

Fable 5 additionally verified the `queue: max` requirement directly against GitHub's documented concurrency semantics (the default `queue: single` cancels pending runs) and confirmed via `gh api` that this repo currently merges release PRs by squash (so the `HEAD^` bug was latent, not yet triggered) while rebase merge remains enabled in repo settings.

## Not in scope / not changed

- No `neuralSPOT-X` release was performed or requested.
- `uv.lock` and the dependency registry are unchanged (verified via `uv lock --check` and `git diff --stat`).
- Exact-commit CI, immutable annotated tag creation, GitHub/PyPI publication, and R

body:
## What changes

Ships the external verification procedure that found the Windows defects, and
records what that run measured.

- `scripts/external-environment-verify.sh` — source-only, not packaged.
- `docs/current/external-environment-verification.md` — procedure, boundary, and
  the recorded Windows 11 run.
- Inventory entry for the new doc.

## Why

Until 2026-08-05 every measurement in this repository had been taken on one
machine. The first run anywhere else found three defects that single-machine
measurement could not surface:

- a skipped ast-grep convention reported as a violation, fabricating ten
  findings pointing at `.persona/conventions` rather than at any source file;
- `@ast-grep/cli` installed but unusable, because `node_modules/.bin` is not
  always on PATH and Node cannot spawn the Windows `.cmd` shim;
- `bootstrap backend` unable to succeed at all, because `O_DIRECTORY` and
  `O_NOFOLLOW` do not exist there.

All three are fixed (#197, #198). The script that found them existed only as a
scratch file, so the capability would have been lost.

It installs a packed tarball into a throwaway project and runs nineteen checks
across environment, fresh install, ast-grep availability, bootstrap, doctor
honesty, Java detection, and the adversarial gate paths. Repository source is
never consulted, so the result reflects what a consumer receives rather than the
working tree.

## What this is careful not to claim

The doc says it plainly: this is a **reproducible procedure, not an independent
audit**. Running it does not establish who ran it. An audit that requires
independence — #116 — still has to record the operator separately, and a
maintainer running it is a maintainer self-check.

**No platform claim is added.** The support matrix, the README platform table,
and `scripts/check-supported-node-matrix.mjs` are untouched. That checker still
refuses a Windows matrix job, which is the project's own encoded decision not to
claim Windows. One host, one Node version, one manual run does not overturn it;
whether the policy should change is a separate decision with its own evidence.

author: hashimthearab
body:
Moves the verification tooling built during the 1.26.40 migration into the repo and runs it in CI, so the checks that found real wire bugs by hand keep running automatically.

## Why

Mojang's schemas are a good skeleton but are not authoritative about bytes. Getting 1.26.40 correct took **147 corrections across 100+ schemas**, and essentially none were discoverable from the docs alone — each came from comparing against a working implementation:

- fields marked `required` that actually carry a presence byte (`ChangeDimension`, `Transfer`, `PlayerAuthInput`) — every one desyncs the packet
- `DimensionDefinition` missing its leading identifier string entirely
- `Compression` on an 8-bit field meaning a raw byte in one packet and a varint in another
- array-level serialization options that actually apply to the elements

Without a gate, the next one is found by desyncing against a live server.

## How it works

Three deliberately separate stages:

1. `valentine_gen --emit-wire-manifest` walks the **resolved IR** and writes each packet's fully flattened wire operations — asking the generator what it emits, rather than parsing generated Rust (the earlier approach stalled at every nested type and left 142 packets unchecked).
2. `extract_gophertunnel.go` reads gophertunnel's `Marshal` methods with `go/ast`, recursing through helper types. No module resolution, no downloads.
3. `compare.mjs` diffs them per packet: `AGREEMENT` / `DIVERGENCE` / `UNRESOLVED` / `NO_ORACLE_PACKET`.

## The gate

Fails when a packet diverges and is **not** in `expected-divergences.json`, and when agreement drops below a floor (catching packets sliding from verified to unverified). Every accepted entry carries a reason, so "known divergence" can't quietly become "any divergence". The five current entries: one genuine oracle conflict (`HurtArmor`), one comparator-granularity false positive (`SubChunk` — Mojang documents a 2D 16×16 height map and we emit exactly that; gophertunnel stores it flat), and three nested camera/biome payloads pending per-field work.

I verified the gate both ways: it passes on the current baseline and exits 1 when an entry is removed.

## Two workflows

- **`wire-conformance.yml`** — runs on PRs touching the generator or this tooling. Asserts the oracle's `CurrentProtocol` matches the pin *before* comparing, since comparing across versions is meaningless.
- **`update-protocol-docs.yml`** — watches the Mojang docs branch recorded in `.gitmodules`, regenerates, and opens a PR **only if conformance still passes**. It deliberately tracks the pinned per-version branch rather than `main`: Mojang's `main` is a later protocol (2169) than live servers accept, and following it would advertise a version that gets rejected.

## Notes

- Oracle pins are **commits, not branches**, in `oracle-pins.json`. A branch citation silently rots — that invalidated pinned overrides twice during this migration.
- Cloudburst stays an optional local cross-check. Its absence can never turn a divergence into an agreement, and it's stale for some packets (`PlayerAuthInput` still inherits v766's bitmask), so silence means *no evidence*, not agreement.
- **Unresolved is not agreement.** 51 packets sit behind gophertunnel interface methods (`ItemInstance`, `EntityMetadata`) the extractor can't follow yet; gophertunnel implements them, the tool just can't read them. ~13 are runtime branches that can never be checked statically — only a live connection settles those.

author: nykefleym-pbi
body:
## Summary

On phones the app looks right, but on iPad / laptop / desktop the mobile-proportioned UI stretched — full-screen backgrounds and overlays spanned the whole wide viewport. Now non-mobile viewports render the whole app inside a **realistic phone mockup** on a beige backdrop, so it keeps true handset proportions.

## What it does
- **Aspect-locked phone (9:19.5):** height fills the window (capped), width is *derived* from it — so it never goes squarish on a short window (measured **2.17** at 1280×800 and 1440×900, matching mobile's 2.16).
- **Overlays stay inside the phone:** the frame is a `position: fixed` containing block (via `transform`), so every full-screen route overlay resolves to it. Radix/Vaul dialogs, sheets, drawers & alert-dialogs are portalled into the frame through a shared container context (`components/frame-portal.tsx`).
- **Beige animated backdrop:** the home-tab `bg-poke-cream` with Poké Balls + type-coloured discs drifting at randomised, wildly-varying speeds (`components/desktop-backdrop.tsx`), reusing `PokeballSpinner` + the type colour map. Respects reduced-motion.
- **Phones untouched:** gated on `useIsMobile()` + `isStandalone()`. Real phones and installed PWA render full-bleed exactly as before — the frame falls back to the old centered 480px column and children use `display:contents`, so mobile markup is byte-identical.

Two viewport-relative sizings that would break inside a width-capped frame were re-based on it: the share-card takeover fills its containing block via `inset-0`, and the Pokédex card width is capped at `--frame-width` (also more correct on mobile).

## Testing
- `tsc --noEmit` clean; full suite **988 passing**.
- Verified with headless Chromium at 1280×800, 1440×900 (desktop frame + drifting backdrop, correct 2.17 proportion) and 390×844 (full-bleed, no frame — identical to today).

author: rolker
body:
## Summary

Adds an opt-in reorder/jitter buffer so a packet that arrives only a few ms
out of order is held briefly and published in order, instead of being
hard-dropped by the `drop_stale_packets` gate (#33).

Closes #35

- **`RemoteNode::admitOrBuffer`** — 3-way `Admit`/`Drop`/`Buffer` decision.
  A sequence gap buffers the packet **without advancing the high-water mark**;
  at-most-one held packet per topic; a gap-filler is published ahead of the
  released held packet; a newer arrival flushes the held one.
  `admitForPublish` is unchanged and remains the admit+advance primitive.
- **`RemoteNode::flushExpiredBuffer`** — hooked into the existing per-remote
  loop in `UDPBridge::spin_once`, so held packets age out on the 10 ms tick
  even when the link is idle.
- **`reorder_hold_window_ms`** — new global node parameter (`double`, default
  `0.0` = disabled, clamped 0–500 ms). With the default, the hot path is
  byte-for-byte identical to pre-#35 behavior. Documented in
  `.agents/README.md` and `config/example_params.yaml`.
- Buffer is cleared on remote-restart detection in `update(BridgeInfo)`.
- Both new methods take an injected `rclcpp::Time now` for fake-time testing.

### Recorded design decisions

- **Global parameter, not per-topic**: deviates deliberately from the
  `remotes.<r>.topics.<t>...` nesting suggested in the issue review — matches
  the `drop_stale_packets` precedent; per-topic tuning is deferred to the #34
  opt-in infrastructure.
- **Inline age-check on the drain tick, no dedicated timer**: hold-window
  release is quantized to the 10 ms `spin_once` cycle, which is acceptable for
  the single-digit-ms reorder case this targets.

## Test plan

- New `test_reorder_buffer.cpp` gtest suite (12 cases, injected fake time, no
  real-time sleeps): gap→buffered without high-water advance; gap filled in
  window → both published in order; window expiry → release on flush;
  at-most-one overflow; restart clears buffer; disabled path unchanged.
- Full suite on the branch: **140 tests, 0 failures** (15 gtest targets; also
  corrects the stale test inventory in `.agents/README.md` — two pre-existing
  targets were never listed).

## Review trail

Pre-push local review (deep mode): **approved**, Round 1, Ship: recommended —
no must-fix findings. Three open suggestions carried into this PR for
reviewer visibility:

1. `admitOrBuffer` decision-rule docstring omits the equal-to-mark `P==H`
   admit case (code covers it inline) — `remote_node.h:236`.
2. No occupancy diagnostic for `reorder_buffer_` (bounded ≤1/topic, ≤500 ms;
   observability nice-to-have).
3. `reorder_buffer_` is not cleared on `on_deactivate` — a held packet would
   release as a slightly-stale publish on next activation. Consistent with
   existing cross-activation state persistence, but flagged for an explicit
   maintainer decision.

Full timeline (issue review → plan → plan review → implementation → pre-push
review) in `.agent/work-plans/issue-35/progress.md` on this branch.

author: nicholmahania-spec
body:
Phase 6 was gated on **evidence, not on code existing**: *"twenty real assets — including one CMYK print PDF, one photographic mockup and one outlined logo — run through it, and the false-positive rate is judged acceptable against your own eye."* That run had never happened.

It has now — and then an adversarial pass took most of the headline back off it. **Both are in this PR**, because the inflated version is the one a reader would otherwise trust.

## The run

Six real client files — five CMYK print PDFs and one 11-artboard Illustrator logo — rendered page by page and sampled through the production path. **22 renderings, 19 readable** (the 3 unreadable are blank artboards, and saying so is the correct answer).

| test | what it checks | result |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | one brand's artwork vs the palette **typed from its own brand guide** | **0 findings / 9** |
| **B** | the same artwork vs a renderer-calibrated palette | **0 findings / 9** |
| **C** | each page of a piece vs that document's own colours | **0 / 16 — and worthless** |
| **D** | each piece vs a **different project's** palette — *should* fire | **68 fired / 68 that can fire** |

**Honest headline: 0 false alarms on one brand's correct work, and every check that could fire, did.**

## What the adversarial pass removed

I first published *"0 false positives in 34 checks, 89% detection."* Both halves were overstated.

- **Test C cannot fail.** It builds each palette out of the colours it then checks — deduped at ΔE00 < 5, compared at > 15. Swept across thresholds it fires zero above 3. So 16 of the 34 "checks" carried no information, and the real false-positive evidence is **nine renderings of one brand**, measured twice.
- **The sample is pseudoreplicated.** 22 renderings hold only **18 distinct colour payloads**; three pages of one document are byte-identical. Test A's n=9 is one brand sheet plus eight artboards of one logo — one brand, the same two inks nine times. ([Hurlbert 1984](https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2307/1942661) is the canonical statement of this error.)
- **The "8 misses" were 2 renderings, not 8 failures.** Each was checked against four foreign palettes. Both are *structurally mute* — strongest colour 2.3% and 7.7%, under the 10% floor — so they cannot fire against any palette at any threshold.
- **The threshold is a band, not a number.** Every value from 12 to 15 gives an identical result here. Below 12 false alarms appear; at 16 detection falls. Choosing 15 buys headroom at the cost of a wider blind spot — a judgement, not a measurement.
- **This is a large-error detector.** Median firing distance ~50 ΔE00; anything 5–15 from the nearest brand colour is reported by nothing. ISO 12647-7 treats a spot colour as out of tolerance around 2.5. The gap is deliberate (the sampler's own JPEG noise floor is 4.17) — but *"the colour half is done"* was the wrong sentence for it.

## The frozen run never touched the sampler

It replays stored vectors through `markColourReading`, so it re-executes none of the stage that produced them. Six sampling mutations left the acceptance tests green. Two are now closed, each verified by re-applying the mutation:

```
STEP 24 → 1     defeating bucketing left ALL 175 tests passing. The existing
                quantisation test passed for an unrelated reason — its smear has
                five distinct values, so mergeNearDuplicates folds them back
                afterwards. A real smear has hundreds, and the coverage floor is
                applied BEFORE merging. New test now fails on the mutation.

smoothing on    sampleImage.js says in its own header that this INVENTS COLOURS,
                and nothing checked it. New e2e uploads fine red/teal bands; with
                smoothing on the panel reports #8e3230 and #395f59 — present
                nowhere in the artwork.
```

`SAMPLE_MAX_EDGE` and `isBackgroundTint` remain uncovered, and `PHASES.md` says so rather than leaving it implied.

**One advocate claim I checked and rejected:** it reported that neutering `isSubstrate` slips through. It doesn't — five tests fail.

## The CMYK problem is smaller than the alarm band

Their guide prints `#ED1C24`; the same ink renders as `#ff2e17` — ΔE00 **6.14**. Test A compares straight across that gap and fires nothing, because the threshold is 15. `calibratedPalette` stays correct and stays unused: it solves a problem this pipeline doesn't have, and the upload path takes already-converted raster.

## What is NOT done

- **The font half.** Phase 6's scope says outlined type carries no font name and silence must not read as clean. Nothing checks fonts, and no PDF can reach the app (uploads accept `image/*`).
- **One asset, not a library.** There is no Asset Library; the mark is the only brand asset with an upload.
- **No photographic mockup** was in the sample, so the false-positive rate is unmeasured against photography.

## Also in this PR

Phases 1a–4 marked done in `PHASES.md`. Business model decided: the client-facing side carries the designer's **own studio branding**, added when ready — not "Powered by". One consequence deliberately **not** applied: `prefs.hidePackWatermark` defaults to `false`, so client-facing output still carries a Creative Companion credit unless the Deliver toggle is found. That contradicts the decision but changes what real clients see, so it's the owner's call.

## Checks

1054 unit tests, lint 139/139, e2e green, build clean. Version 3.47.2.

author: olvchae
body:
## 무엇을

웹 배포 워크플로의 VM 스텝에서 `/home/<user>/.env` 를 덮어쓰던 한 줄을 제거했습니다.

```diff
- sudo echo ${{env.ENV}} | base64 --decode > ./.env
```

더불어 이제 쓰이지 않는 `ENV_KMJ/KEC/NPR` 주입 3줄도 함께 제거했습니다.

## 왜

`/home/<user>/.env` 는 **백엔드(feelio-api) 워크플로가 쓰는 런타임 설정 파일**입니다. DB 접속·JWT secret·OAuth client secret 이 여기 들어갑니다. 웹과 API가 같은 VM에 배포되면 **나중에 배포한 쪽이 상대의 설정을 통째로 날립니다.**

두 레포 모두 `ENV_KEC` 라는 **같은 이름**의 시크릿을 쓰지만 내용은 완전히 별개입니다:

| | feelio-api | feelio-web |
|---|---|---|
| `ENV_KEC` 갱신일 | 2026-08-04 01:02 | 2026-08-04 08:20 |

그리고 웹은 이 파일이 애초에 필요 없습니다. `Dockerfile` 이 `nginx:alpine` 으로 정적 파일만 서빙하므로 런타임 환경변수를 읽지 않고, `VITE_API_BASE_URL` 은 빌드 스텝(`APPLICATION_SECRET`)에서 이미 번들에 박힙니다. 즉 이 한 줄은 **얻는 것 없이 백엔드만 망가뜨리는 순수 부작용**이었습니다.

실제로 배포 환경에서 구글 소셜 로그인이 `invalid_client: The provided client secret is invalid` 로 실패 중이며, 이 덮어쓰기가 유력한 경로입니다.

## 어떻게 테스트했는지

- `npx js-yaml .github/workflows/main.yml` — 워크플로 YAML 파싱 통과
- `npm run build` — 통과 (`✓ built in 411ms`)
- `npm run lint` — `ProfileModalDc.jsx:483 'e' is defined but never used` 1건이 뜨는데, **이 PR 이전부터 main 에 있던 오류**입니다. 이 PR 은 `.github/workflows/main.yml` 만 건드리므로 무관하며, 범위 밖이라 손대지 않았습니다.

## 머지 후 필요한 후속 조치 (순서 중요)

1. **이 PR 머지 후에** `feelio-web` 의 `ENV_KEC` / `ENV_KMJ` 시크릿 삭제
   > ⚠️ 순서를 바꾸면 안 됩니다. 시크릿을 먼저 지우면 `${{env.ENV}}` 가 빈 값이 되어 `.env` 를 **빈 파일로** 만들어버립니다.
2. `GCP_VM_HOST_KEC` 값이 두 레포에서 동일한지 확인 (현재 갱신일이 api 08-05 / web 08-04 로 다름)
3. `feelio-api` 의 `ENV_KEC` 안 `GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET` 을 올바른 값으로 갱신 후 재배포

### Motivation
- Make the video title extractor resilient to newer YouTube DOM patterns (lockup/view-models) and to accessible attributes like `title` and `aria-label`.
