author: joshrotenberg
body:
Works toward #81.

## What is in the way

Building a connection is 240 lines inline in `run()`: `if --demo`, else match on HTTP or stdio, with bearer tokens, headers, OAuth profile resolution, import approval, and profile lookup threaded through. It calls `exit_with_error` at roughly a dozen points.

That last part is the crux. Every failure currently ends the process, which is right for startup and wrong for a command typed at a prompt: a mistyped URL must not take the session down with it.

## Plan

**1. Extract the connection.** A function that takes a resolved target and returns `Result<Connected, String>` instead of exiting, where `Connected` carries the client, the optional reconnect `Connector`, and the label the prompt and banner use. `run()` keeps its current behaviour by reporting the error and exiting; the new command reports it and stays.

**2. Parse a target once.** The command line already accepts an HTTP URL, a `path:entry` selector, a profile name, `--demo`, or a stdio command. `connect` should take the same things in one argument, so a target is parsed in one place rather than two.

**3. Swap the live session.** `Session` already replaces its client under a running REPL for reconnects, and `refresh_surface` already refetches into the same `Arc<RwLock<Surface>>`, so the machinery exists. What has to follow a switch: the surface, the prompt's server name, the surface-change subscription, and the job registry, which belongs to the server that issued those task ids.

**4. Decide what survives.** Aliases and history are the operator's and should. Captured variables hold results from a server that is no longer there; carrying them silently would let `$x` mean something stale, so they are cleared with a line saying so.

## Scope

This PR does the four steps above, so `connect` works from a session that already has a server.

**Starting with no server at all is a follow-up**, and #81 stays open for it. Today `session` is an `Arc<Session>` that every command reaches through; a disconnected state means it can be absent, and each of the 14 `client()` call sites has to answer for that. That is a second change of similar size, and worth landing separately from the extraction.

Fixes STATS-421

Follow-up: STATS-423 (register the affected events in Tracks with owners and descriptions, and run the STATS-421 verification query — `blog_id_pct` ≥ 95 — after deploy).

## Why
Stats upsell impression events were not carrying the blog_id parameter, which prevented them from being tied to specific sites for impact measurement. Without blog_id, it's impossible to measure impression-to-purchase conversion and determine if upsells are reaching the right audience.

## Changes
Added blog_id parameter to all stats-related tracking events:
- Upsell impression events (stats_card_upsell_view)
- Notice viewed, dismissed, and CTA/support click events (commercial/free site upgrade, do you love stats, GDPR, tier upgrade, free plan purchase success)
- Upsell page and modal events (stats_upsell_*, stats_upsell_modal_*)
- Purchase flow events (checkout redirect, personal/commercial flows, purchase notices, upgrade sliders)
- Date control events (date picker opened, date range applied, shortcuts) — including gated clicks via the onGatedHandler implementations
- Date range navigation and chart type selection events
- Feedback panel, card, and modal events
- Locations, posts, devices, and UTM module events
- Promo card and mini-carousel view/click/dismiss events
- UTM builder and empty-state action events

Mini-carousel and promo-card view events keep the pre-existing `site_id` key alongside the new `blog_id` for data continuity. The purchase-page upgrade-source attribution event now waits for a resolved site ID and fires at most once.

Deliberately left alone: `calypso_jetpack_module_toggle` — its schema is shared with non-stats producers (site-settings) that also omit blog_id; changing only the stats emitters would fragment the event.

## Testing
- Verified all tracking calls now include blog_id parameter
- Confirmed code follows existing patterns in the stats module
- All formatting and linting issues resolved

author: sfc-gh-dachristensen
body:
## What

Adds a `pg_lake_table.fast_drop_file_cleanup` GUC (off by default). When enabled, dropping a writable, **default-location** Iceberg table queues the table's **entire location prefix** as a single `is_prefix` deletion-queue row, instead of reading the table's Iceberg metadata and enumerating every referenced file. `VACUUM` then removes everything under that prefix in one recursive pass.

> #539 has merged, so this now sits directly on `main`. The dependency on it is real rather than textual — see [Interaction with #539](#interaction-with-539).

## Why

The normal drop path walks `metadata.json → manifest lists → manifests → data files` in object storage and inserts one deletion-queue row per file. For tables made up of many files, that walk — and the per-file rows it produces — dominate the cost of the drop.

Managed tables already live under a unique per-table prefix (`…/<table>/<relationId>`), so their storage can be reclaimed by deleting that one prefix without touching any Iceberg metadata. This is the "fast delete" the prefix layout already makes safe.

#509 (merged) made the *removal* of individual objects much cheaper by batching S3 `DeleteObjects`. What remains expensive, and what this PR avoids, is the metadata walk itself plus inserting and later draining one queue row per file — so the two changes address different halves of the cost.

## Behavior / safety

- **Off by default**, so nothing changes unless a caller opts in.
- **Managed (default-location) tables only.** A custom `location` may be shared with other tables, so `TryMarkTablePrefixForDeletion` declines for those and the drop falls back to the existing per-file enumeration — nothing outside the table is ever deleted.
- Ordering of the drop's cleanup strategies is now: fast (prefix) → deferred (`defer_drop_file_cleanup`, metadata-resolve) → eager per-file. A table created in the current transaction takes none of these (its in-progress files are cleaned up separately).
- `previous_metadata` is skipped on the fast path since the prefix delete already covers it.
- The existing whole-prefix fallback (used when the metadata walk fails for a managed table) is unchanged; this reuses the same `InsertPrefixDeletionRecord` / `is_prefix` machinery, now as a first-class opt-in.

## Interaction with #539

`InsertPrefixDeletionRecord` queues the row with `table_name = 0`, so no per-table vacuum pass ever claims it — only the dropped-table pass (`VacuumRemoveDeletionQueueRecords(InvalidOid, …)`) does. Before #539 that pass ran only from a manual `VACUUM (ICEBERG)`, so a fast drop left the prefix queued until someone vacuumed by hand. #539 added `VacuumRemoveDroppedTableFiles()` to `PgLakeIcebergVacuumForTables` and to its catch-up pass, which is what makes the autovacuum worker reclaim it.

One caveat worth recording: #539 charges the per-vacuum budget by files *removed* rather than rows claimed, and a prefix row appends exactly one entry to the deleted-path list however many objects it removes. So a prefix delete costs 1 unit of `max_file_removals_per_vacuum` regardless of size. That is pre-existing behavior for prefix rows — this PR just makes them common — and bounding prefix deletes is explicitly deferred to #538.

No file overlap between the two branches; the code touched here is entirely in `pg_lake_table/src/ddl/`.

## Measured impact

Benchmarked against the eager (default) and `defer_drop_file_cleanup` paths on the test-suite moto server, counting object-store requests alongside wall time since local latency understates real S3. Medians of 3 reps.

The win is driven by **snapshot count**, not file count: the eager walk costs `1 + 2 × snapshots` sequential round trips. For a table written by many small commits (the mirror/CDC/streaming shape) at 512 commits:

| mode | drop s | drop reqs | vacuum s | vacuum reqs | total s | total reqs |
|:-----|-------:|----------:|---------:|------------:|--------:|-----------:|
| eager | 6.743 | 1025 | 0.314 | 4 | 7.057 | 1029 |
| defer | 0.027 | 0 | 7.109 | 1029 | 7.135 | 1029 |
| fast | 0.026 | 0 | 0.569 | 9 | **0.595** | **9** |

- The DROP itself: 6.74 s → 26 ms, and flat in the file count rather than linear.
- End to end, including the VACUUM passes that actually reclaim the storage: ~12× faster and ~114× fewer object-store requests.
- Deferral is not a substitute — it relocates the identical walk into VACUUM.
- Countervailing cost: the prefix VACUUM is slightly more expensive than draining known keys (0.569 s vs 0.314 s) because it has to LIST the prefix. That is 0.26 s against 6.7 s saved.
- A table bulk-loaded in a single commit sees no measurable end-to-end gain (0.094 s vs 0.093 s at 256 files): one snapshot is only 3 requests to walk, so there is nothing to save.
- Every mode left 0 objects under the prefix, so the fast path is not trading correctness for speed.

## Tests

Three tests in `test_drop_table.py`:
- `test_fast_drop_queues_prefix` — default-location drop queues exactly one prefix row, no per-file or resolve rows; files survive the drop; `VACUUM` removes the whole prefix and drains the queue.
- `test_fast_drop_custom_location_falls_back` — with the GUC on, a custom-location table declines the prefix path and falls back to per-file enumeration (no prefix row).
- `test_fast_drop_prefix_reclaimed_by_autovacuum` — the autovacuum worker reclaims the prefix with no manual `VACUUM`, covering the #539 dependency above. This test fails on `main` without #539.

These sit alongside the existing control tests (`test_normal_drop_enumerates_control`, `test_deferred_drop_skips_enumeration`, `test_custom_location_is_also_deferred`).

Ran locally on the rebased branch: `test_drop_table.py` (25 passed) and `test_deletion_queue_batching.py` (6 passed). CI is green.

Docs: added a note to the "Dropping an Iceberg table" section of `docs/iceberg-tables.md`.

body:
Appointment DML Boundary **PR B2** — lifecycle, audit-invariant and cross-tenant behavioural coverage.

Test-only "verify and pin". Builds no command, changes no application behaviour, creates no migration.

## 1. Base and head

| | |
|---|---|
| Production base SHA | `03e7deaa38a7646a1f19a3d883c0a2b07894cec0` (`claude/build-hone-saas-hOex7`) |
| B2 head SHA | `f09634877556615da7be3af1cacd068e2731f06f` |
| Branch | `test/appointment-lifecycle-audit-invariants` |
| Worktree | `~/Hone-DML-B2` |

Branched from production, **not** from PR #522. B1 and B2 are independent and have zero file overlap.

## 2. Changed files (5)

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| `tests/db/appointment-lifecycle-commands.db.test.ts` | **new** — T6.1–T6.7 |
| `tests/db/appointment-audit-invariant.db.test.ts` | **new** — T5.1–T5.6 |
| `tests/db/cross-studio-isolation.db.test.ts` | extended — T4.1–T4.4 |
| `tests/db/public-booking-concurrency.db.test.ts` | mis-named test corrected + title-truthfulness guard |
| `tests/app/calendar/appointment-lifecycle-mark-complete.test.ts` | extended — T6.8 only |

`3211 insertions, 4 deletions`. `tests/db/helpers/harness.ts` was **not** touched — every fixture is local to the new files, so `full_matrix_required` is not set (`npm run ci:plan` classifies this diff as `application` + `database`).

## 3. No-change confirmations

* **No migration.** `npm run migration:state` → repo max `0171`, hosted max `0171`, next free `0172`. **`0172` was not created.**
* **No schema change**, no `create/alter/drop` shipped in this branch.
* **No application source change.** The only non-`tests/db` file is a test under `tests/app/calendar/`.
* No E2E/Playwright spec added. No browser lane run.
* No production connection, no linked Supabase command (this worktree has no `supabase/.temp/project-ref`, so a linked command is structurally impossible here). Local stack only: `postgresql://postgres:postgres@127.0.0.1:54322/postgres`, project `Hone-0162`.
* Nothing merged, nothing deployed. PRs #517–#522 untouched; no other worktree opened.

## 4. Lifecycle-command case matrix (T6.1–T6.7)

`mark_appointment_complete` (0032:4052) · `mark_appointment_no_show` (0033:334) · `practitioner_cancel_appointment` (0033:241) — these had **no behavioural test anywhere** before this PR.

| # | Case | Expected |
|---|---|---|
| T6.1 | complete, practitioner of another studio | raise `42501` `'practitioner is not an active member of this studio'` |
| T6.1 | complete, inactive practitioner of own studio | same |
| T6.1 | **positive control** — active non-owner member completes | `completed`, 1 audit row |
| T6.2 | complete, unknown appointment id | raise `P0002` `'appointment not found'` |
| T6.2 | complete, appointment in another studio (actor legitimately active in the supplied studio) | identical `P0002` |
| T6.2 | the two failures are byte-identical | no existence oracle |
| T6.3 | complete from `cancelled` / `no_show` / `completed` (past-dated) | `P0002` `'appointment is not confirmed (current: …)'` |
| T6.3 | complete, confirmed but `ends_at` in the future | `P0002` `'appointment has not yet ended'` |
| T6.3 | **positive control** — past confirmed | `completed` + exactly one `marked_complete` |
| T6.4 | cancel: foreign actor / inactive actor | `not_authorized` |
| T6.4 | cancel: id exists nowhere | `not_cancelable` |
| T6.4 | cancel: **real appointment in another studio** | `not_cancelable` |
| T6.4 | cancel: `completed` / `no_show` source (future-dated) | `not_cancelable` |
| T6.4 | cancel: confirmed but already started | `not_cancelable` |
| T6.4 | cancel: future confirmed, owner actor | `cancelled`, `cancelled_by='owner'` |
| T6.4 | cancel: future confirmed, **non-owner** actor | `cancelled`, `cancelled_by='practitioner'` |
| T6.4 | cancel twice | `already_cancelled`, **no second audit row**, first reason preserved |
| T6.5 | no-show: foreign / inactive actor | `not_authorized` |
| T6.5 | no-show: `cancelled` / `completed` / `no_show` source | `wrong_status` |
| T6.5 | no-show: id exists nowhere | `wrong_status` |
| T6.5 | no-show: **real past confirmed appointment in another studio** | `wrong_status` |
| T6.5 | no-show: confirmed, `ends_at` future | `too_early` |
| T6.5 | no-show: past confirmed | `marked` + one `marked_no_show`, cancellation columns still NULL |
| T6.6 | EXECUTE grant matrix | see §6 |
| T6.7 | 21-case refusal sweep | whole-row + audit-count no-op |

**Every sentinel exercised.** `practitioner_cancel_appointment`: `not_authorized`, `already_cancelled`, `not_cancelable`, `cancelled` — all four. `mark_appointment_no_show`: `not_authorized`, `wrong_status`, `too_early`, `marked` — all four. `mark_appointment_complete` returns `void` and signals refusal by raising; both its SQLSTATEs (`42501`, `P0002`) and all three of its distinct messages are asserted.

> **Doc correction.** The audit's §12.2 B2 summary lists a `too_late` sentinel. No such sentinel exists in either 0033 command; the started-appointment refusal is `not_cancelable` (0033:287). Also, `practitioner_cancel_appointment` returns `not_cancelable` (not `not_authorized`) for a row it cannot find, and `mark_appointment_no_show` returns `wrong_status` — both documented branches the audit's §14 T6.4/T6.5 rows omit. All are now covered.

## 5. Rollback / no-op invariants (T6.7)

`expectUnchanged` compares **`to_jsonb()` of the entire appointments row** — all 57 columns — plus the `appointment_audit` row count. It is deliberately not a hand-picked subset: a command that cleared `cancellation_token_hash` or bumped `sync_version` on its way to returning a sentinel would evade a 7-column check.

The sweep covers **21 refusal branches — 7 per command**. The three "appointment id exists nowhere" branches are excluded by construction (there is no row to leave unchanged) and are asserted inline in T6.2/T6.4/T6.5 instead; the guard's title says exactly that rather than claiming blanket completeness.

## 6. EXECUTE-grant results (T6.6)

Signatures resolved from the migrations' own `revoke`/`grant` statements (0032:4099, 0033:314, 0033:392), not guessed, and each verified to resolve via `::regprocedure`.

| Function | PUBLIC | `anon` | `authenticated` | `service_role` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `mark_appointment_complete(uuid, uuid, uuid)` | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ | ✓ |
| `mark_appointment_no_show(uuid, uuid, uuid)` | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ | ✓ |
| `practitioner_cancel_appointment(uuid, uuid, uuid, text)` | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ | ✓ |

Three hardening points, each added after the adversarial pass:

1. **PUBLIC is measured with `has_function_privilege('public', …)`, not only `aclexplode(grantee = 0)`.** Measured on this stack against a throwaway default-privilege function: with `proacl IS NULL` the aclexplode count is **0** while `has_function_privilege('public', …)` is **true**. An aclexplode-only probe therefore cannot distinguish "revoked" from "never granted, so PUBLIC holds the default EXECUTE". The test now also asserts `proacl IS NOT NULL`.
2. **Exactly one overload per name** is asserted. A probe is per-oid; a later migration adding an overload would create a new oid carrying Supabase's `ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES` grant to `anon`/`authenticated`/`service_role` while every signature-bound probe stayed green (the miss CLAUDE.md §5 records twice).
3. **The real-invocation probe uses `asUser`, not `asRole`.** `asRole` always rolls back, which would make its post-state assertion structurally incapable of failing — a granted EXECUTE would let the SECURITY DEFINER function run to completion and the rollback would erase the evidence. `asUser` commits, so the mutation would persist and be caught. The probe also asserts the message matches `/permission denied for function/i` and **not** `/active member of this studio/i` — mandatory, because `mark_appointment_complete` raises `42501` itself, so SQLSTATE alone cannot tell "EXECUTE denied" from "the function ran and refused the actor".

## 7. Audit invariants (T5)

**T5.1 split, deliberately.** The audit groups eigh

## Summary

- Replaces ~19 call sites that inline-ternary'd `err instanceof Error ? err.message : fallback`, or hand-rolled a local APIError-body unwrapper duplicating `web/src/lib/errors.ts`, with the shared `errorText(err, fallback)` helper.
- Sites that already had genuinely distinct handling (status-code branches for 403/409/etc.) keep that logic; only the final non-APIError fallback line now delegates to `errorText`.
- No visual/layout changes — this is logic-only, so no `design.pen`/Pencil pass.

## Behavior change

`errorText` unwraps an `APIError`'s JSON body (`{error}` or `{message}`) into a more useful message where the site previously only had `err.message` (which for an `APIError` is the raw `"${status}: ${body}"` string). Concretely:

- `web/src/routes/AdminLogs.tsx`, `web/src/routes/AdminSettings.tsx` (×5), `web/src/routes/CreateServer.tsx` had *no* prior APIError unwrapping at these sites — displayed error text can now show the unwrapped JSON message (or the raw body, without the `"<status>: "` prefix) instead of `err.message`.
- `web/src/components/registry-browser.tsx`, `web/src/components/server/CloneServerDialog.tsx`, `web/src/components/server/ServerActionsCard.tsx`, `web/src/routes/tabs/{Modpacks,Mods,Settings,Players}.tsx`, `web/src/routes/tabs/settings/Access.tsx` already had local APIError-unwrap helpers duplicating `errorText`'s logic — collapsed to a one-line delegate; behavior is unchanged there except `errorText` also checks a `message` field in addition to `error`.
- `web/src/routes/tabs/settings/Networking.tsx`'s dual-mutation error picker now uses truthiness instead of `instanceof Error` to select between the save/remove mutation errors (equivalent, since `APIError extends Error` and the mutation's error type is `Error | null`), then unwraps via `errorText`.

author: arohou
body:
## The problem

If any program other than ChimeraX is listening on the MCP bridge's port, the
bridge reports that every command succeeded while nothing happens at all.

I hit this with a stale mock server left running on port 8080 that answered
`200` with `{}` to every request. An agent asked to open a structure and a map,
style the volume and set the view. All four commands came back
`"Command completed successfully"`. ChimeraX had never been launched — and was
never even looked for.

Three fail-open steps compound:

1. `is_chimerax_running()` GETs `/cmdline.html` and returns `response.status
   == 200`. Any 200 means "ChimeraX is running here."
2. `_execute_command_request()` gets a 200 with parseable JSON, finds no
   `error` key, and returns empty return values, JSON values and logs.
3. `format_chimerax_response()` has nothing to report and falls through to the
   literal string `"Command completed successfully"`.

Auto-start never fires, because it hangs off `aiohttp.ClientConnectorError` and
a squatter *answers* rather than refusing the connection.

Port 8080 is `DEFAULT_CHIMERAX_PORT` and also the default for webpack, Flask,
Jenkins, Tomcat, Spring Boot and countless dev stubs, so this is easy to hit by
accident. The failure is silent, which makes it worse than a crash: an agent
confidently reports work it did not do.

## The fix

- **`is_chimerax_running()`** additionally requires `/cmdline.html` to actually
  be ChimeraX's page. I kept probing the static file rather than switching to
  `/run`: static files are served straight from the request handler thread,
  whereas `/run` is dispatched onto the UI thread via `session.ui.thread_safe`,
  so a busy ChimeraX would fail a `/run` probe and get a redundant second
  instance started underneath it.

- **`_execute_command_request()`** rejects a 200 that lacks `rest_server`'s
  JSON-mode envelope, raising a new `PortNotChimeraXError`. `_run()` always
  emits `json values`, `python values`, `log messages` and `error` in JSON
  mode, so this is a reliable invariant.

- **`run_chimerax_command()`** handles that exception like a refused
  connection, so ChimeraX gets started elsewhere. One case is carved out: if
  the port really is ChimeraX whose REST server was started without
  `json true`, it reports how to fix it (`mcp start`) instead of spawning a
  duplicate instance.

- **`start_chimerax()`** no longer exempts the default port from its
  availability check. That exemption was the reason a squatted 8080 could not
  recover: ChimeraX was sent off to bind a port it could never get, and the
  launch simply timed out. Now the bind test runs for every port and a taken
  one moves to the next free port.

- **`find_best_chimerax_instance()` / `check_existing_rest_server()`** consult
  instances this bridge started before sweeping the fixed fallback list. Once
  we can land on an arbitrary free port, the fixed list alone can no longer
  find our own instance, and each subsequent command would start another
  ChimeraX. The fallback list is now a single `_FALLBACK_PORTS` constant rather
  than being spelled out in three places.

Net effect: a squatted default port becomes invisible. ChimeraX starts on the
next free port, the command is retried there, and the user sees a normal
result.

`format_chimerax_response()`'s `"Command completed successfully"` string is
deliberately unchanged. Once the envelope is known to be genuine, an empty
result is legitimate — `view` and friends really do log nothing.

## Tests

New `src/bundles/mcp_server/tests/test_bridge_port_conflict.py`, 11 tests using
small stub HTTP servers on ephemeral ports; no ChimeraX session required.
Covers an imposter answering `{}` to everything, a real JSON-mode ChimeraX, a
real ChimeraX with JSON mode off, a dead port, the default-port availability
check, and candidate-port ordering.

Seven of the eleven fail against the current code; the other four are
no-regression controls that pass either way. The central one fails with
`DID NOT RAISE` — that is the bug.

## Verification

Beyond the unit tests, checked against real ChimeraX instances on macOS:

- Squatted default port: probe rejects the imposter, the bind test moves to the
  next port, ChimeraX launches there, the command is retried, and a real PDB
  opens as model #1 with genuine chain-info logs.
- Real ChimeraX started with `remotecontrol rest start port N` (no `json
  true`): produces the "run `mcp start`" error, with `start_chimerax`
  instrumented to assert it is never called.
- Healthy default port: still discovered and driven exactly as before.

## Note

The module docstring advertises `CHIMERAX_REST_HOST` and `CHIMERAX_REST_PORT`
environment variables that the code never reads. That is a genuine doc/code
mismatch and a useful escape hatch on a busy machine, but it is independent of
this bug, so I have left it for a separate PR to keep this diff focused.

author: osirison
body:
Closes #169. Six commits, four modules, all measured out of the 51 fixtures F8 extracted rather than by re-reading the prototype — which is the harness paying for itself one task after landing.

| module | what it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `ui/controls.js` | 11 button kinds × 6 size rungs, inputs, toggle, 17px checkbox, pill tabs, day chips, stepper, radio cards, the typed-`DELETE` gate |
| `ui/rows.js` | transfer row (in-flight / queued / compact), five flat rows (history, path, fact, pass, action), the deletion card |
| `ui/bands.js` | attention band, destructive band, never-synced band, consent panel |
| `ui/dialog.js` | the overlay layer — sizing, scrim, focus trap, patch-not-rebuild |

## Three things worth a reviewer's attention

**The transfer row's arrow is beside the seam, and two documents say otherwise.** `03-main-screen.md` says *"the arrow is on the outside edge in both columns, pointing away from the seam"* — contradicting its own preceding sentence, which gives the element order correctly. Issue #169 repeats the wrong gloss. All four frames that draw it (dark and light, full and compact) put the `→` last in the leaving column and the `←` first in the arriving one, so both hug the centre line. Frames win under §1.3. The rule lives in a pure `transferSlotOrder()` with its own test, because a screen built from the prose still looks plausible and the style gate cannot catch it until S1 maps the frame. §53

**Mirroring is not one rule.** The transfer row keeps its arrow *inside*, beside the seam; the deletion card's severity eyebrow puts its dot *outside* and flips the row's alignment with it. Two rules, opposite directions, one screen apart. There is deliberately no shared `side` helper — the next person to write one will make them agree, and one of them will then be wrong.

**Only three of the seven "overlay" routes are dialogs.** F4's table is right about routing but says nothing about presentation. `conflicts`, `deletions` and `armed` are full 1042×764 windows that keep the header and the four doors; wrapping them would put a scrim over a window with nothing behind it. `routes.js` now carries `presentation`, with tests. §57

## Three defects found by building on top of earlier work

- **`--decision-bg` / `--decision-border` were one token pair holding two different bands** — its dark value measured off the attention band, its light value off the recoverable deletion card, because no light frame draws the attention band at all. Nothing consumed it yet, so nothing rendered wrong; it would have broken the moment `bands.js` reached for it, in one theme only. Split by site, the same move §43 made for `--chip-attention-border`. §52
- **The one drawn checkbox disagreed with `controls.css` in six places** — surfaced by the consent panel coming out 2.5px short. Two are load-bearing rather than cosmetic: the box is transparent because it sits on a crimson tint, and its border is `--text-5` not `--line-inert` (that is the unselected *radio* ring). §55
- **The deletion card's eyebrow wore a class with no rule behind it** and rendered at 16px sans instead of 10px uppercase crimson. Caught by rendering, not by reading.
- **The dialog layer's own `onMain` rewrite put a home button on onboarding** — `onMain` had two callers and the dialog work only reasoned about one. Not a cosmetic slot: `routes.js` says the takeover cannot be dismissed, and the app mark is the home affordance now that onboarding has no footer nav, so it was a working door out of a flow that is not supposed to have one. Found by review, fixed in `dddfbf4`, verified by driving the app into the takeover with a stubbed `firstRun` status and reading the header back. §57a

## Verification

`rows.js` and `bands.js` have no style-gate coverage until S1–S7 stamp `data-fid`, so every component was built in a headless page and its computed styles compared against the fixture values — including the failed pass row at 1000×84 against the frame's 1000×84 with its −12px bleed, and both deletion cards down to the `.16` vs `.20` facts divider. Bands were re-run under `prefers-color-scheme: light` to confirm every tint resolves through the right token.

`dialog.js` was verified behaviourally instead, which is where its risk is: the main screen stays mounted underneath, the header does not rearrange (see the fourth defect above — this was true for main-plus-dialog and false for onboarding until `dddfbf4`), the node survives two poll cycles unchanged, Tab stays inside, Esc closes it exactly once through F4's chain, and focus returns to the door that opened it.

## Chosen values a designer should confirm

Three, all documented as chosen rather than left to look measured, all with their derivation written down:

- the **light attention band** (§52) — no light frame draws it
- the **light never-synced band** (§54) — likewise
- the **scrim** (§56, filed open) — not one frame in the bundle shows a dialog over a screen, so unlike the other two there is no drawn analogue at the same site, only a proportion borrowed from `--shadow-dialog`

## Deliberately not built

`4a Compact`'s deletion rows are not the deletion card at a smaller size (332×61, no facts strip, no gate, no second button) — that is F6, and it needs two compact band alphas no token carries yet. `5a Plan`'s `8px 2px` border-**bottom** row rung is S4's. The history row has no Phase-1 consumer at all — S5 omits the block until G1 lands a per-path history query — but it is drawn, measured and built, so the gate can check it the day the query exists.

Gates: 41 tests, `check-tokens` ok (113 tokens, 90 themed, both light blocks agree), fidelity 2067 assertions / 0 failures, copy 224/224, `fidelity:stale` (51 fixtures still match the prototype), `fidelity:determinism` (52 identical files), lint and format clean.

author: robertcdawson
body:
## Why

The episodes read as AI-written, and transcript analysis across all 67 published episodes showed the problem is structural formula, not stray filler words:

- The outro opened with the identical "**Pull back and look at today's stories… and a pattern emerges: the gap between…**" skeleton for 9 consecutive episodes ("Pull back" 21×, "the gap between" 21×)
- The sign-off collapsed into a "**Keep your X and your Y**" Mad Lib (31 occurrences, with near-verbatim repeats), preceded by the fixed "That's the {bulletin/signal/briefing} for {date}"
- Beats were announced by name: "the honest caveat" 37×, "worth noting/watching" 52×, "the takeaway" 19×
- 45/67 intros used the same two-move template (shock fact → "It's {date}, and today's episode is stacked: [list]")
- Persona noun banks saturated the corpus: "signal" 158×, "dispatch" 29×, "frequency" 18×

Root causes: the JSON schema descriptions prescribed the exact beat list and a "find a pattern across the stories" outro (and the schema wins over the prose instruction to vary), the prompt asked for a "fresh sign-off" with no structural guidance, and the model never saw its own recent prose.

## What changed

**`src/script.ts`**
- Rewrote the `intro`/`segments[].chunks`/`outro` schema descriptions to grant beat-order and shape variety instead of prescribing a checklist and a synthesis outro
- Added deterministic per-day `INTRO_MOVES`/`OUTRO_MOVES` rotation (salted `stableHash`, independent of the persona rotation), injected as "Today's opening/closing instruction" in the user prompt
- Hard-fail validators for the high-precision outro molds: "pull/step/zoom back" opener, "a pattern/thread/frequency emerges/runs through", "Keep your X and your Y", "That's the {bulletin} for {date}", and outro-scoped "the gap between". Every hard regex has a mirror sentence in the prompt so a compliant model can't hit it
- Closed the semicolon evasion in the split-contrast validator ("That's not X; that's Y" now caught)
- Soft-banned the announced-beat tics via `BANNED_SCRIPT_PHRASES` ("the honest caveat", "worth noting", "the practical takeaway", …)
- Detoxed the two personas whose delivery text literally supplied the recycled radio vocabulary; added a global rule capping radio-metaphor nouns at one per episode
- Demoted `gpt-4o-mini` to last-resort fallback (it ignores the voice-rule block; the weakest published episodes line up with its fallback days) and bumped attempts per model 2 → 3 so a mold hit can re-roll

**`src/ledger.ts` + `src/index.ts`** — recent-prose feedback loop
- `loadRecentStyleSnippets` parses the last 8 transcripts already on disk into intro-opener / outro-opener / sign-off snippets (non-blocking, `[]` on any failure)
- Injected into the user prompt as a `RECENTLY USED — do not reuse or lightly rephrase` block (~800 input tokens/day, zero extra API calls) and included in the script stage-cache key

**`scripts/diagnose-openrouter-script.ts`**
- New real-episode replay mode: `EPISODE_DATE=<published date> npm run diagnose:script-model` rebuilds the story clusters from that day's sidecar curation records, includes the recent-style block, and prints the generated script — so prompt changes can be A/B'd against actually-published transcripts

**Tests** — new `test/script.style.test.ts` (mold validators positive/negative, semicolon contrast, move determinism, RECENTLY USED injection), transcript-parser tests in `test/ledger.test.ts`, and synced assertions in `test/script.persona.test.ts`

## Verification

- `tsc --noEmit` clean; all script/ledger test files pass (50/50). The only failing unit tests locally are pre-existing ffmpeg-missing environment failures in `audio.stingers` / `tts.request`, unrelated to this change
- Ran the snippet parser against the real `docs/episodes` transcripts: it extracts openers/sign-offs cleanly, and 7 of the last 8 outros it surfaced are the exact molds the new validators now reject
- Live A/B needs an API key (not available in this environment): run `EPISODE_DATE=2026-08-05 npm run diagnose:script-model` with old vs. new prompt and compare intros/outros
- Post-deploy check over the next ~5 episodes: `grep -ciE "pull back|the gap between|keep your .* and your|honest caveat|worth noting|a (pattern|thread|theme) emerges" docs/episodes/<date>.transcript.txt` should approach 0, and watch logs for `script.model_fallback` / validation-retry churn

author: owenpriceskelly
body:
## Summary

Two latent bugs in `scripts/nightly_smoke_test.pbs` meant every PBS chain ran exactly one generation, then died silently — generation 2 crashed before its payload and never scheduled generation 3.

**Bug 1 — self-path breaks at generation 2.** The script located itself via `$PBS_O_WORKDIR`, which is only the submit directory for the *first*, human-submitted generation. For a job submitted *by another PBS job*, `PBS_O_WORKDIR` is the parent job's cwd — `$HOME`, since PBS starts jobs there and the script never `cd`s. Generation 2's `qsub` of the bogus `$HOME/...` path fails, and `set -euo pipefail` kills the job before the smoke-test runs. Fix: each generation passes the path down explicitly with `qsub -v SELF_PATH=...`; the existing `${SELF_PATH:-...}` default already honors the override. `CLUSTER` rides along in the same `-v`, since PBS doesn't propagate the environment down the chain and shared installs (sophia/polaris) need it on every generation — previously it would have silently reverted to the manifest default from generation 2 on. `-v` passes only the listed variables, so nothing else about the job environment changes.

**Bug 2 — duplicate-chain guard never matched.** The guard used `qselect ... -s Q`, but a job submitted with `-a` sits in state **W** (waiting), not Q, so the guard was a no-op. Fix: `-s QW`.

Also corrects the guidance that went with them, in the script header and `docs/nightly-smoke-testing.md`:
- Stopping a chain: look for the **waiting (W)** job, not a queued (Q) one.
- Fast end-to-end test: override `RESCHEDULE_AT` (via `qsub -v`) so generation 1 schedules generation 2 a few minutes out — that exercises the actual handoff. The previously suggested `qsub -a <time>` on the kickoff only delays generation 1's own start and tests nothing about the chain.

The SLURM sibling (`nightly_smoke_test.sbatch`) is unaffected: it recovers its path from `scontrol show job` and SLURM propagates the submit environment by default.

## Test plan

- `bash -n` on the edited script.
- The fixed pattern (explicit `-v SELF_PATH` handoff + `QW` guard) is lifted from a sibling self-scheduling chain script developed against ALCF; the running Sophia/Polaris chains will be re-kicked-off with per-cluster copies of this fix, which exercises the generation 1 → 2 handoff for real.

Fixes #249.

Ports `mypy.typeops.is_literal_type_like` to the `type_kernel` Rust extension behind the `native_type_kernel` gate.

A pure scalar predicate (LiteralType / UnionType / TypeVarType walk), no `TypeInfo`-field reads, so the existing wire format fully covers it. The Rust returns `None` for any form it cannot decode (notably `TypeAliasType`) and the Python shim defers to `get_proper_type`, matching the strangler-fig per-call gate used by `is_duplicate_mapping` (#247) and the checkexpr scalar queries (#208).

Semantics mirror typeops.py:1241-1257 exactly: uses `any(...)` over union/typevar items (not `all`).

Consumers (checkexpr.py:2334/3735, checker.py:5035/7032/7163) route through the typeops module gate, so no call-site changes.

## Coverage
- 9 new Rust unit tests in `typeops.rs` (`literal_type_like_*`): literal true / instance false / union-of-literals true / union-mixed true-via-any / typevar-bound true / typevar-values true / alias defers (None) / callable false.
- Gate-on parity: `TEST_NATIVE_TYPE_KERNEL=1` full `testcheck.py` = **8144 passed** (7 failures are the known py314 TString native-parser baseline #235, matching unpatched master).
- The shim gate uses no `_native_typeops_resolver` (Rust path does not need the snapshot for this predicate), consistent with `is_literal_type_like` needing only the decoded type.

Files: `crates/type_kernel/src/typeops.rs` (+193), `crates/type_kernel/src/lib.rs` (+1), `mypy/typeops.py` (+7), `stubs/type_kernel.pyi` (+2).

author: appsciences
body:
Closes #1.

`dev-backup.sh` mirrored `~/dev` into iCloud as a loose file tree, left `~/.claude` uncovered entirely, and produced nothing you could hand to a new machine. This adds a `--zip` mode that builds one archive with paths relative to `$HOME`:

```
cd ~ && unzip -o dev-backup-<stamp>.zip
```

**2.5 GB mirror → 596 MB archive**, built and integrity-verified in 48 seconds.

## What's in it

Full source for every project, complete `.git`, per-project `.claude/` config, and Claude Code's global config plus accumulated memory. Dependencies and build output are excluded — `npm install` / `pub get` / `pod install` rehydrates them. A generated `RESTORE.md` ships inside the archive.

## What changed

| | |
|---|---|
| `--zip` mode | Stages both sources locally, compresses, runs `zip -T`, and only then moves into iCloud so the sync daemon never sees a partial file. Staging is a true mirror, so repeat runs copy only what changed. **Mirror mode stays the default** — no silent behavior change. |
| `claude-backup.filter` | Allow-list for `~/.claude`. That tree is 195 MB of regenerable session state around ~360 KB of hand-authored config; a deny-list would silently bloat as new cache dirs appear. Credentials are never included — auth lives in the macOS Keychain. |
| `fed-docs/` | Excluded. 1.4 GB of video and photos, not code. |
| HTTrack mirrors | Detected by their `hts-cache/` marker rather than by name, condemning the whole mirror root (149 MB today). |
| `.claude/worktrees/` | Excluded. 4.1 GB of throwaway checkouts whose branches all live in `.git`; verified to hold no real work. |
| `postgres_db/`, `pgdata/` | Excluded. A file-level copy of a running cluster can capture a torn state — use `pg_dump`. |

## Bug fixed along the way

The gitignore scan pruned a bare `node_modules` but not renamed copies like `node_modules 11.48.10 AM`, so it descended into them and emitted **thousands** of malformed patterns for paths git had quoted. Pruning `node_modules*` and passing `core.quotePath=false` cuts the generated set from thousands to **54**.

## `.git` is still never excluded

An audit of the 56 repositories under `~/dev` found **6 with no remote at all** and **21 holding unpushed commits, local-only branches or stashes** — 264 MB that exists nowhere else. Dropping `.git` would have saved 174 MB and risked all of it.

## Tests

`dev-backup.test.sh` builds a synthetic `~/dev` and `~/.claude` covering every filter case, runs a real archive build, and asserts on the resulting zip. **27 assertions, all passing**, including:

- a **tracked** `build/` directory survives (the deskreen case the gitignore-driven scan exists for)
- a restored repository passes `git fsck` and resolves `HEAD`
- the renamed-`node_modules` case that caused the bug above

Verified against the real tree as well: restored `notedude-web` is clean, tracking `origin/main`, `fsck` reports 0 errors, exec bits preserved, all 5 custom agents and 50 memory files present.

## Note

`.env` files **are** included (79 of them) — projects will not run without them. Treat the archive as containing secrets. `RESTORE.md` says so explicitly.

author: legofsalmon
body:
One verified correctness fix from the review, in `hub.ts`.

**Stacked on tranche 2 (#45).** Its files overlap tranche 2's, so this PR is based on `claude/review-tranche-2` to keep the diff clean — you'll see only the two files below. When #45 merges and its branch is deleted, GitHub retargets this to `main` automatically. Merge #45 first.

## The bug

`onHello` marks the user online on **every** hello, but the `close` handler decrements presence exactly **once** per socket. So a client that sends `hello` twice on the same connection — a retry, a reconnect that reused the socket, or simply a misbehaving client — left the online tally inflated by one. After that socket closed, the user showed as "online" with no socket behind them at all. `hello` isn't one of the verbs the flood guard covers, so the inflation could also be walked up deliberately.

Presence is user-visible (the online dots, the "who's here" list, the remote/on-site badge), so a leaked count is a real, if quiet, wrongness — a ghost crew member who never leaves.

## The fix

`onHello` now increments at most once per connection:

- **First hello** → bring the user online (as before).
- **Repeat on an already-authed socket** → presence-idempotent; the tally doesn't move.
- **Re-auth as a different identity** on the same socket (unusual, but possible) → move the one count off the old id and onto the new, so `close`'s single decrement still balances.

It reuses the existing `markOnline`/`markOffline` pair (which already keep `online`, `localSockets`, and the presence broadcasts in step), so the on-site/off-site badge logic is unchanged.

## Verified

New test in `server/test/sync.test.ts`: a repeated hello on one socket, then close, must return the online tally to zero — it fails on the old code (the tally sticks at 1) and passes now. Full server suite green (**429**), lint, `prettier --check`, `tsc --noEmit -p server` all clean.

## On the rest of the review's server findings

While assembling this I re-verified the other flagged server mediums/lows rather than take the labels on trust, and several didn't hold up as worth a change:

- **`/api/search` "N+1"** — real in form (an `isMember` call per hit, ≤50) but negligible in fact: in-process SQLite index lookups on a cold, user-initiated action. Pushing visibility into SQL would duplicate `channelAudience`'s public-or-member logic in raw SQL, where getting it subtly wrong leaks private/DM messages into search — not a trade worth making. Left as-is.
- **Rate-limit shared behind NAT** — crew connect directly to the box on the LAN (distinct IPs); this only bites multiple *remote* users behind one NAT through the tunnel, and loosening the PIN-guess limiter trades away brute-force protection. Judgment call, not a bug. Left as-is.
- **Wildcard cert → localhost origin** (`index.ts`) — already handled: `certNames()` filters wildcard names, so the origin already falls back to localhost. (Noted in #47.)
- **PTP grandmaster across domains** (`ptp.ts`) — a real accuracy gap (one ledger across all PTP domains can read two legitimate domains as an election war), but the correct fix is a per-domain redesign of the clock-status contract and panel. That runs against the file's own rule ("left until real captures exist"), so it's parked against the "capture real packets" task rather than redesigned blind. Single-domain — the common case — is already correct.

author: lilith
body:
This decoder reads untrusted input, so a panic on a malformed bitstream aborts a caller that cannot catch the unwind. A typed error is the correct outcome. That is a robustness argument — a panic in safe Rust is a controlled unwind, not memory corruption, and I am deliberately not dressing it up as a security class it does not belong to.

## The discovery mechanism was the first problem

`tests/fuzz_sweep.rs` only did bit flips, truncation and splices — all of which leave a mostly-valid arithmetic stream, so the symbol decoder barely saw hostile values. Added a HOSTILE TILE PAYLOAD op (keep the headers, replace the tail with PRNG bytes) and one more. Deep-error reach is now **~50%** across three independent seeds (60k and 2×500k iterations), against a pinned floor of 10% — 5× margin, deterministic in (seed, iterations).

## Converted (reachable from crafted input)

- `av1_ss_size_lookup` has no valid chroma plane size for some luma shapes. libaom rejects that with `AOM_CODEC_CORRUPT_FRAME` (`decodeframe.c:393-401`); the port `assert_ne!`d, justified by "the roundtrip never produces them" — a claim about our encoder, not about attacker input.
- Two `debug_assert_ne!`s that hid the same failure in **release** as an anonymous `MAX_TXSIZE_RECT_LOOKUP` index-out-of-bounds.
- An error message that hedged between a SHORT file and a CORRUPT one under one category; `ReadBitBuffer` gained `mark_syntax_error(field)`.
- Named the panics whose message told a caller nothing (convolve, lpf_scalar, three bare `unreachable!()` in intra predictors, cdef_frame preconditions).

## Five anti-vacuous contract tests

Including: no committed POC may reach `DecodeError::Internal` (that variant means decoder bug, so one reachable from input is a defect — 11 POCs).

## Deliberately not done

- Did NOT churn the ~35 fixed-array `try_into().unwrap()` bounds-check-elimination sites — the hot kernels are built on them.
- Did NOT convert provable invariants into dead error paths.
- Did NOT touch the encoder's 126 panic sites — reviewed only far enough to confirm none is bitstream-reachable; aom-encode is a trusted-input API.
- Drafted a conformance over-rejection finding about the 4:2:2 chroma guard and then **retracted it**: libaom has a second, ungated check at `decodeframe.c:1359-1371` in exactly the place the port makes it.

Verified: 1001/1001 tests in BOTH dispatch modes, 235/235 conformance vectors / 274/274 frames byte-identical port==C==golden, zero new clippy diagnostics vs baseline.

*(Terminology corrected in `dacf164` on the stacked branch: an earlier draft of this description and several in-tree comments called these panics a "denial of service". That was inflated and has been fixed to say what is actually true.)*

author: ccam80
body:
Preview of the updated selective-fastmath PR before it goes live as a superseding PR; the preface and this line are dropped from the upstream text.

---

Fastmath now accepts individual flags for eight LLVM flags + ftz.

Fastmath flags provided as bool | set | dict | FastMathOptions in a @cuda.jit() decorator are respected by the compiler. This brings the MLIR backend past parity with numba-cuda, which accepts the flags but treats any truthy flag as a blanket fastmath=True.

fastmath=True or {"fast"} applies all flags but nnan/ninf, as numba-cuda and nvcc --use_fast_math do. nnan/ninf can still be applied if named explicitly. Each device function compiles under the flags included in its own decorator.

Fastmath-capable arith/math ops are identified from the generated bindings, and get stamped with #arith.fastmath<...>. fast division and tanh get rewritten manually (as in numba-cuda) to __nv_fast_fdividef and tanh.approx.f32. Constant-zero powers are folded to 1.0 before lowering. flush-to-zero is not applicable at function level, so is applied module-wide through the libnvvm/ptxas flags.

This PR passes the module-level libnvvm/ptxas flags to libnvvm through a new CAPI parameter. The flags were also dropped at the linker boundary, so they are added to the linker config. nvJitLink expects an integer option form (-ftz=1) and cuda.core provides a word form (-ftz=true), so there's a LinkerOptions subclass added to translate bool-int.

Piping `contract` through allows fma uplift to take place in the compiler, so the `math-uplift-to-fma` pass in the base pipeline is no longer required. Removing this early uplift allows ptxas to perform some cse before contracting, and afforded a ~5% cycle count and ~23% SASS instruction count improvement on a large, inline-heavy kernel in our package (CC 8.9, LTO on).

Tests:
- test_fastmath.py: {"arcp"} gives div.approx, {"nsz"} keeps precise division (no blanket truthiness), {"afn"} gives sin.approx without approximate division, invalid flags rejected, attributes appear in MLIR, standalone {"ftz"} compiles and emits .ftz instructions, LTO links succeed, nvJitLink options made numeric, lineinfo/debug flags with fastmath keep debug directives and div.approx.
- test_array_reductions.py: NaN-aware reductions stay correct under fastmath=True.
- test_math.py: x ** (0.0) and x ** (-0.0) return 1.0 for NaN, +/-0.0, +/-inf bases under fastmath=False, {"afn"}, and True.

Verification (CC 8.9, Windows): 24/26 xfailed fastmath tests go green, 2 stay xfailed (fastmath doesn't propagate into device functions from decorated kernel, no ZeroDivisionError); GPU fast-vs-precise results agree to within float32 roundoff on a float32 test kernel.

author: tvolodi
body:
Closes #498.

`ci.yml` had three `continue-on-error: true` steps. **A step that can fail without failing the build is not a gate — it is a log line.** Each was added with a written exit condition. Two of those conditions had already been met, but the masks were never removed.

## 1. `transition.zig in-file tests`

> *"Reported, not gated, until #428 closes; then drop continue-on-error."*

**#428 is CLOSED**, and `zig build test-transition` **exits 0**. The mask outlived its reason.

This is the one that matters most: `src/engine/transition.zig` is the pure-function core that CLAUDE.md forbids all I/O in. A regression there was being reported and ignored.

## 2. `Test isolation`

> *"222 pre-existing BLOCKERs ... flip to a hard gate once that backlog is cleared."*

Inaccurate twice over:

- The real count is **184 BLOCKER + 41 MAJOR**, not 222 BLOCKER.
- That backlog is **already suppressed by the baseline** — it was never what made this step fail.

The step failed on exactly **3 findings** in `tests/integration/helpers.zig` whose **line numbers had drifted**. The baseline recorded them at 388/393/394; they now sit at 432/437/438. `issue_key()` is `severity|code|file|line|message`, so a line shift silently breaks suppression.

Root cause: **PR #490 (`8103072`) moved those lines without resyncing the baseline.** Confirmed by checking out `8103072` and reproducing the identical 3 findings — before any commit on this branch existed.

## 3. `Install Zig` — unchanged, correct as-is

Keeps its `continue-on-error`. It's a fallback pair, and the following `Confirm Zig is on PATH` step hard-fails if both the action and the direct download fail, so a mirror outage cannot silently pass.

## Baseline resync — verified to hide nothing new

Before regenerating, I diffed fresh findings against the old baseline on `(severity, code, file, message)` — ignoring line:

| | Count |
|---|---|
| Findings added | **0** |
| Findings removed | **0** |
| Entries whose line changed | **3** |

The `regeneration_note` now records that procedure, so the next line shift gets resynced rather than re-masked.

## Verification

- Both newly-gating steps exit 0
- The three sibling linters in the same job still exit 0
- `ci.yml` parses; exactly **1** `continue-on-error` remains (`Install Zig`)
- **Mutation-checked:** dropping one entry from the baseline makes the isolation gate exit **1**; restoring it returns **0**

## Related

Filed [#497](https://github.com/tvolodi/R-Co/issues/497)/ISS-0170 separately: CI jobs are cancelled after ~15 min waiting for a runner and render as a red X indistinguishable from a real failure. Across the last 40 runs — 31 success, 6 cancelled, 3 failure — only 3 are genuine code failures. That defect fabricates false red; this PR fixes the opposite problem of hiding real red.

author: sinhasagar01
body:
Ten units of work were built, measured and reported as merged. Each was merged with `git merge --no-ff` into **local** `main` and its branch deleted. Nothing was pushed and no pull request was ever opened, while `origin/main` sat 22 commits behind.

Nothing was lost. The code is intact and now pushed. **What failed was the record.**

## The diagnosis

**Every instrument in this repo reads the working tree, and the working tree was correct.** ralph passed, the census passed, the join passed, the build was green. The claim that failed was about a system none of them look at — so ten instances passed unnoticed, not because a check was weak but because **there was no check, and its absence was invisible from inside every gate that exists**.

And the tell was in the output every time: `git merge` prints nothing on success, so "it worked" was a signal **supplied rather than observed** — the same family as a mutation reporting SURVIVED because it never applied to its subject.

## The gate

`ralph/tests/upstream.mjs` asserts both halves.

- **A1** local `main` is not ahead of `origin/main`
- **B1** HEAD is covered by a merged pull request — a pushed `main` with no PR is this same failure one step later

It needs the network, so it is skipped **by name** in `run.mjs` beside `parity` and `studio-type`, printed in the summary rather than silently absent.

`8457d46` is pinned as the one declared exception — **pinned to that exact commit, not to a range**, so the next uncovered commit fails. A range-shaped exception would have let the eleventh instance through.

`B1b` originally asserted `KNOWN_UNCOVERED_TIP.length === 7` — a tautology about a constant the file declares, the exact family #368 swept for. It now checks the pin still resolves.

## Verification

ralph 2564 across 62 suites, `upstream` 5/5 separately, lint and tsc clean.

author: rfrenchseti
body:
Migrates `pdschecksums`/`pds4checksums` and `pdsinfoshelf`/`pds4infoshelf` onto the shared core, and fixes six latent defects in them. Plan: `plans/2026-07-25-modernization-plan.md`, PR-26 (Phase 6). Full record with every measurement and command line: `critiques/pr-26-validation.md`.

## What this does

All four tools hand-rolled the same `main()`: the same parser, the same log setup, the same walk from a command-line path to a list of (unit, selection) pairs, and the same loop. That work is now shared, and each tool is its domain functions plus `SPEC`, `TASKS` and a short `main()` — the pattern `pdsarchives.py` already demonstrates.

These four do **not** run on `run_main`, and that is deliberate. Their targets carry a file selection, their log path is one of two methods chosen per target, and the two kinds of tool finish differently: an infoshelf run's status is its exit code, while a checksums run may still have a chained `pdsinfoshelf` command to execute and — by pinned current behavior, `support.TOOLS_WITHOUT_EXIT_STATUS` — deliberately does not report its own logged errors in its exit code. Serving both from one driver would have meant exactly the boolean shrug-flags the data-only `ToolSpec` rule forbids. So they run on a second driver, `_shelf_common.run_selection_main`, which **returns** rather than exits and leaves each tool its own epilogue.

## `_common.py` split into per-family modules

Deferred entry 98 decided this structure and its trigger: one file until the first family whose extraction takes `_common.py` past the 1,000-line limit, which splits it, the driver staying put. The measurement crossed here — `_common.py` reached **1,081** lines — so the split happened, on the measurement rather than on the projection:

| module | lines | holds |
|---|---|---|
| `_common.py` | 339 | `ToolSpec`, the command line, `run_main` — what every family shares |
| `_archives_common.py` | 241 | the archive family |
| `_shelf_common.py` | 529 | the checksum and shelf family, including the new driver |

Entry 98's rate-based projection (~1,318 lines) was too high: these pairs are mostly domain functions that stay in their tool modules. PR-27 should re-derive it rather than reuse it.

## Behavior changes — six, each with a test that fails without its fix

`pdsinfoshelf`'s validation compared `checksum1 != checksum1` and `abs(modtime1 != modtime2) > 1`. Neither branch could ever fire. Measured at this PR's base, a `--validate` run over a tree where a file's content **and** modification time had both changed reported `File info matches` for that file and exited 0.

1. **A content change is reported again** — `checksum1 != checksum2` (pds3 infoshelf).
2. **A modification-time change is reported again** (pds3 infoshelf).
3. **The child-count message names both counts** — it formatted `(count1, count1)`, so `Child count mismatch 7 7` now reads `7 6` (pds3 infoshelf).
4. **A chained run's exit code arrives intact, and its arguments are not word-split** (pds3 checksums). This is what `os.system` → `subprocess.run` actually buys, and it is not cosmetic. `os.system` returns a wait status — the exit code shifted left by eight — and `sys.exit()` truncates that to the low byte, so *every* nonzero exit code of a chained `pdsinfoshelf` run was reported as success. Separately, `' '.join(new_list)` handed the command to a shell unquoted, word-splitting any holdings path containing a space. Both measured; both pinned. Two further consequences of the same line are enumerated in the record without tests: `subprocess.run` **raises** where the shell reported a target it could not execute, and `system(3)` ignored SIGINT in the caller where `subprocess.run` does not.
5. **A path that expands to no targets finishes instead of raising** (both checksums tools). `proceed` was assigned only inside the target loop, so an empty volume set directory ended the run in `UnboundLocalError`.
6. **The modification-time comparison changes pds4's results too** — which the plan does not say. Both flavors truncated to the second before comparing, so pds4's working comparison was string equality on quantized values. Truncation is a quantization, not a tolerance: its verdict turns on where the second boundary falls rather than on how far apart the times are. The comparison is now one shared function that parses both times and allows one second, the convention `validate_tuples` already uses on epoch seconds. Over the values these tools produce the new mismatch set is a **subset** of the old, so nothing that passes today starts failing. Approved by the owner on 2026-08-06 conditional on the new results being more accurate, and enumerated here rather than left to land as a silent improvement.

   **One qualification, added after review, because the first version of this claim was too tidy.** The class that stops being reported is `|Δ| ≤ 1 ∧ floor(t1) ≠ floor(t2)`, not "false positives". It is mostly boundary-straddle noise, but the tolerance is inclusive — the form the plan prescribes and the form `validate_tuples` uses — so a file whose modification time moved by **exactly** one second is now reported as matching, and on pds4 that is a detection the old truncation made. Measured: a label shifted 1.0 s validates clean, the same label shifted 1.5 s reports the mismatch. Left as specified and recorded as deferred observation 120 so `<=` versus `<` can be decided on its merits.

**The fix reaches a second tool, which the plan does not mention.** `pds3/re_validate.py` calls `pdsinfoshelf.validate()` directly at `:152` and `:183`, so changes 1, 2 and 6 change what `re_validate --infoshelves` reports — and that is the scheduled tool, with `--batch` and `--error-email`, which mails whenever any error is logged. Measured on a sandbox volume with a byte-changed, mtime-shifted label and refreshed checksums: base reports nothing, head reports five errors. Volumes a nightly `re_validate` called clean will generate error mail on the first run after this merges, without those volumes having changed. That is the fix working, but it is an operational consequence and belongs in the enumeration.

The three tests PR-13 wrote to pin defects 1–3 as current behavior are inverted here, which is what its module header says they were written for. No test was skipped, xfailed or deleted, and no golden or baseline was edited.

### Log and output text — two lines

Under the Phase 6 rule, and both enumerated line by line in the record:

- A traceback inside one of these tools now names the shared driver's frames rather than the tool's own `main()`. Unavoidable — a traceback names the frames on the stack — and identical in kind to the one PR-25 enumerated. The comparison below deliberately normalizes traceback **line numbers** and **not** file names, which is what makes this visible rather than hidden.
- The two infoshelf tools no longer `print(sys.exc_info()[2])`, the repr of a traceback object, to stdout. Keeping it would need a flag whose only job is to print a memory address for two of the four tools.

All four tools' `--help` output is **byte-identical** to base.

Against real holdings (`$PDS3_HOLDINGS_DIR` / `$PDS4_HOLDINGS_DIR`, `PDSFILE_TEST_HOLDINGS=full`), at base `56b8823` and at head, comparing per-test id-to-outcome maps rather than counts:

- **`--mode s`**: 558 ids at both, **identical** outcome for every one.
- **A real run of all four tools through every task** — 122 records covering all five tasks, both error paths, `--archives`, a single-file selection, the `--infoshelf` chain in four states, plus log files and written artifacts. A base-versus-base control runs clean at 0 of 122 records, which is what licenses attributing the rest: 18 records differ, 171 lines, **every one attributed**, and **0 artifact r

author: enesyilmazcode
body:
Closes #2.

Exact k-NN by full scan. Deliberately not fast — its job is to be provably right, because every approximate index in this repo is scored by how often it agrees with it. If the oracle is wrong, every recall number downstream is wrong in a way nothing else can detect.

## What's here

- `distance.hpp` — scalar dot product and squared L2, plus a `score` wrapper where larger always means closer, so the selection code never branches on the metric.
- `topk.hpp` — `nth_element`-based partial selection, and `recall@k`.
- `src/brute_force.cpp` — computes groundtruth for a query set and writes `groundtruth.ivecs`.

## Three decisions worth calling out

**The kernels loop over `d_padded`, not `d`.** The pad is zeroed, so it contributes 0 to the dot product and `(0-0)^2 = 0` to the squared L2. That means no remainder handling, and the SIMD kernels in #3 can use the identical loop bound instead of a separate scalar tail.

**The square root is never taken.** `sqrt` is monotonic, so it cannot change a ranking. Taking it would cost time and buy nothing. L2 scores are stored negated so that "larger is better" holds for both metrics.

**Ties break by ascending id, and that is load-bearing.** Clustered data produces exact score ties constantly. Without a deterministic rule the groundtruth file would depend on `nth_element`'s internal pivot choices, recall@k would jitter run to run, and a real regression would be indistinguishable from noise. There's a test that shuffles 500 candidates across 3 distinct scores and requires the same answer.

Selection is `nth_element` then sort of just the k survivors — `O(N)` rather than the `O(N log N)` of sorting all N to read off ten. On a million vectors that difference is the entire query budget.

## Gate

The issue asks that a query equal to `x_5` return id 5 at distance 0.

```
$ ./build/nanorag_brute --k 10 --metric ip
base    20000 x 128
queries 200 x 128
metric  ip   k=10

gate: query = x_5 -> top1 id=5  ip=0.999999821   PASS

scanned 200 queries in 0.277 s  (1.386 ms/query, 14.4 M comparisons/s)
wrote data/groundtruth.ivecs  (200 rows x 10 ids)
```

And on L2, where the distance should be exactly zero rather than approximately:

```
gate: query = x_5 -> top1 id=5  l2sq=0   PASS
```

The `ip` value is `0.999999821` rather than exactly 1 because the vectors are normalized and the accumulation runs over 128 float additions. That is float rounding, not an error.

## Cross-validation

A gate that only checks one query proves very little, so the whole groundtruth file was recomputed independently in numpy and compared:

```
numpy vs nanoRAG, exact order match: True
numpy vs nanoRAG, same id sets     : True
```

All 200 queries, all 10 neighbors, in the same order including the tiebreak. Also verified: the same inputs produce a byte-identical groundtruth file across runs, every id is in range, and no row repeats an id.

## Tests

`tests/test_oracle.cpp`, wired into ctest alongside the layout suite. Covers the kernels against hand-computed values, the `||q-x||^2 = 2 - 2(q.x)` identity that keeps the two metrics consistent on normalized data, selection ordering and the tiebreak under heavy ties, `k > N`, empty input, and recall@k including the short-result case where the denominator must stay `k`.

```
1/2 Test #1: layout ... Passed
2/2 Test #2: oracle ... Passed
100% tests passed
```

## Note on the throughput number

14.4 M comparisons/s is the scalar baseline, and it is meant to look slow. That is the number #3 has to beat.

author: harjothkhara
body:
## What Problem This Solves

Closes #119478.

Streaming an answer that contains many `[` characters re-parses the entire accumulated response as Markdown once per bracket-shaped delta. The work is quadratic in response size and changes nothing — the emitted text is byte-identical with and without it.

Measured through `normalizePlainTextToolCallStreamEvents`, counting characters handed to `resolveProtectedRanges`:

```
response    re-parses    characters re-parsed
10.3 KB          450                 762,430
21.0 KB          900               3,107,155
42.3 KB        1,800              12,589,105
```

Response size doubles, characters re-parsed quadruple. The identical document with `(` instead of `[` costs **zero** re-parses.

This contradicts the expectations pinned in this file's own coverage: `stream-normalizer.test.ts` asserts `resolverCalls` is `0` for ordinary streamed text and `resolvedLengths.length <= 3` once a candidate-shaped delta appears.

## Why This Change Was Made

Tokenizers emit `[` as its own token, so a bracket-dense answer ends many deltas exactly at `[`. At `grammar.ts:203` a bracket opener with no name characters yet produces:

```ts
const firstName = text.slice(firstNameStart, cursor);   // ""
if (cursor === text.length && "tool".startsWith(firstName)) {
  return { kind: "prefix" };
}
```

`"tool".startsWith("")` is true, so a bare `[` is reported as a potential call start. `stream-normalizer.ts` then materializes the whole accumulated response and hands it to `resolveProtectedRanges`.

Tracing one bracket showed three resolutions, only one of them expensive:

```
resolve(len 74)   <- prefix + "["      the whole response, per bracket
resolve(len  1)   <- "["               candidate buffer only
resolve(len 10)   <- "[section-0"      candidate buffer only
```

A bare opener carries no evidence: the empty name matches every tool. The next delta brings the name and settles it against the candidate buffer, which is already cheap. So the fix skips protection resolution for an opener that has no name yet, and changes nothing else.

Protection is still resolved for every candidate that carries name characters, so a real `[read]` is unaffected. Scope is one guard plus a predicate — no change to the resolver contract, the matcher, or the candidate state machine.

## User Impact

Long bracket-dense answers — `[tool.poetry]`, `[Unit]`, pasted `[2026-08-04T…] INFO` log lines, i.e. routine coding-agent output — stop burning CPU proportional to the square of the response.

Protection work becomes linear:

```
response    characters re-parsed     before
10.3 KB                    1,840    762,430
21.0 KB                    3,790  3,107,155
42.3 KB                    7,690 12,589,105
```

Emitted text is byte-identical before and after, at every size.

Honest limits:

- This bounds the *number* of whole-response re-parses; it does not make the remaining ones incremental. A response that genuinely contains many named tool-call candidates still resolves once per candidate.
- Measured as characters handed to the resolver, not wall-clock, so the numbers are deterministic and machine-independent. The issue reports 3.2 s of CPU for the 35 KB case.

**Separate pre-existing defect found while verifying this, not fixed here and not caused by this change.** A fenced tool call whose opener arrives as its own delta has its body silently deleted:

```
input:   ```\n[read]\n{"path":"x.txt"}\n[/read]\n```
emitted: ```\n```
```

The same call in a single delta is preserved correctly. I confirmed this reproduces byte-identically on unmodified `main`, so it predates this patch — the pending-candidate classification resolves protected ranges against the candidate buffer without the accumulated fence prefix, so a fenced call reads as executable. That is user-visible content loss and deserves its own issue; I did not widen this PR to chase it.

## Evidence

Production diff is **+15 net LOC** in one file (tests counted separately):

```
16  1  packages/tool-call-repair/src/stream-normalizer.ts
--- tests ---
39  0  packages/tool-call-repair/src/stream-normalizer.test.ts
```

Proof command:

```
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs packages/tool-call-repair
```

The regression test sits directly beside the two pinned expectations it extends, and asserts the shape rather than a timing: a 4x longer response must not cost more than 8x the protection work, and the absolute cost must stay proportional to the candidates.

**Negative control.** With only `stream-normalizer.ts` restored to `origin/main` and the new test kept, it fails for the right reason:

```
FAIL  keeps protection work linear when streamed text is bracket-dense
AssertionError: expected 6299605 to be less than 2970440
```

With the patch, the same measurement is **7,690**.

**Blast radius**, found by symbol across the whole repo — every consumer of the normalizer:

```
packages/tool-call-repair/src/index.ts
src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt-stream.ts
src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt.tool-call-normalization.ts
src/plugin-sdk/provider-stream-shared.ts
```

```
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs packages/tool-call-repair \
  src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt.tool-call-normalization.test.ts \
  src/plugin-sdk/provider-stream-shared.test.ts \
  src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/stream-resolution.test.ts
-> all shards passed (155 package tests, including every fence-protection case)
```

Typecheck `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p tsconfig.core.json` clean; `oxfmt --check` and `oxlint` clean; `git diff --check` clean.

Reviewed with `codex review --base origin/main`. It raised one P1 — the fenced-split content loss above — attributing it to this patch. Running the same fixture against restored upstream sources produced byte-identical output, proving it pre-existing; it is reported above rather than folded into this diff.

No Crabbox/Testbox on this machine, so cross-OS breadth is CI's.

*AI-assisted: investigated, implemented and proved with Claude Code; the diff and evidence above are human-reviewed.*
