author: ichabodcole
body:
## What this is for

`release-please` triggers only on `push` to `main`. That has **no recovery path**: when a run is blocked, fixing the cause fires nothing, and the only way to re-run it is to push another commit to `main` — a poor recovery mechanism for a release tool, and one that mints an empty commit to do it.

This adds `workflow_dispatch:` so the workflow can be run from the Actions tab.

## Why now — a month of releases silently did not happen

Runs stopped after **2026-07-10** and nothing surfaced it. Every check that would normally catch this came back clean:

| checked | result |
| --- | --- |
| workflow `state` | `active` |
| YAML validity | valid |
| workflow file changed since creation? | **no — unchanged** |
| Actions enabled repo-wide | yes |
| repo visibility | public, so Actions minutes were not the constraint |
| did the merges reach `main`? | yes — PRs **#89** and **#90** both landed |

**Two merges to `main` produced no run and no error.**

## Root cause — a repository setting, not this file

**Settings → Actions → General → Workflow permissions** was set to *"Read repository contents and packages permissions"*.

This workflow declares:

```yaml
permissions:
  contents: write
  pull-requests: write
  issues: write
```

A workflow **cannot widen past the repository default**, so those grants were unobtainable and release-please could not create a branch, open a release PR, or tag.

**The evidence that the setting is a ceiling rather than a default:** this exact file succeeded repeatedly through 2026-07-10 and **has not changed since**. The repository setting is therefore the only variable that moved.

> ⚠ The separate checkbox **"Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests"** was already enabled. It is **necessary and not sufficient** — it permits PR creation specifically, while the radio governs the token's baseline scope. **Both are required.**

## What is queued behind the block

Since `spellbook-v1.16.0` on `main`:

```
feat:   24
fix:    19
docs:  129
total: 190 commits
```

**Expect a minor bump (v1.17.0), not a patch.** If a patch is proposed instead, something is reading a narrower range than this and is worth stopping to check.

## Known limitation, for later

The release PR that release-please opens is authored by `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and **`GITHUB_TOKEN` pushes do not trigger further workflows.** Harmless while release-please runs alone — it will silently break any build or publish step keyed off that PR.

## Note on sequencing

`workflow_dispatch` is read from the **default branch**, so the button does not appear until this is merged to `main`. Merging this PR is itself a push to `main`, so it should fire release-please directly — the button is for the *next* occurrence.

author: ashwinvar
body:
`apiPost`, `apiPut` and `apiPatch` called `res.json()` unconditionally on any 2xx. `res.json()` throws a `SyntaxError` on an empty body, so a **204 No Content** — or any 2xx that arrives empty — rejected the promise and the UI reported a **failed write for a write the server had committed**.

That's the worst shape this class of bug takes: the operator sees an error for something that worked, retries, and on a non-idempotent endpoint the retry is a duplicate.

## Latent, not live — said plainly

**No backend endpoint returns 204 today.** Checked before writing anything:

```
grep -rn "status_code=204|HTTP_204|Response(status_code=" backend/   →  no matches
```

The only `204` anywhere in the tree is a substring of the part number `CNMG 120408`. And a FastAPI handler returning `None` serialises as the JSON literal `null`, which parses fine.

So **nobody is hitting this.** It's a trap laid for whoever adds the first 204 — their endpoint would have looked broken while working perfectly. These tests exist so that doesn't happen.

## The contract

**An empty body resolves to `null`.** Not `undefined` — `null` is already what "the server said nothing" means everywhere else in this file, and it survives `JSON.stringify` if a caller stores it.

## Read as text, don't sniff the status

Checking `res.status === 204` looks equivalent and isn't: a gateway, a proxy, or a handler returning `""` all produce a 2xx with nothing to parse, and a status check still throws on those. **The mutation that makes exactly that mistake is caught by three tests.**

## Two deliberate non-changes

- **`apiGet` stays on `res.json()`.** Every GET in this API returns data by definition, and it's the hot path — the dashboard issues **46 of them every 3 seconds per open tab**. Changing the busiest code in the app to cover a case that doesn't exist isn't a trade worth making. The comment there says so, and says what to do if a GET ever legitimately 204s.
- **`apiDelete` already returned `Promise<void>`** without parsing, so it was never affected.

## On the `as T`

`readBody`'s signature promises `T` and can hand back `null`. The sound alternative is `Promise<T | null>`, which forces a null check at every one of the dozens of call sites that destructure the result — to describe a case that only arises on endpoints returning no body, where the caller isn't reading the result anyway. The unsoundness is the lesser cost, but it **is** one, so it's written down in the function's own doc comment rather than hidden.

## Verification

**Six new tests, two per verb, all failing against master** before the fix.

**Two controls that pass either way**, ruling out the wrong fixes:
- a real JSON body must still come back parsed — otherwise "always return null" passes everything
- a 500 with an empty body must still throw — otherwise every server error becomes a silent success

**4 of 4 mutations caught:**

| Mutation | Caught by |
|---|---|
| revert `readBody` to `res.json()` (the bug) | all six empty-body tests |
| always return null, never parse | both controls |
| status-sniff 204 only | the three empty-**200** tests |
| leave `apiPut` un-fixed | the two `apiPut` tests |

---

**Risk assessment:** low. The changed path is the **success** branch of three write helpers, and only its parsing step. Error handling, headers, the 401 session logic and `apiGet` are untouched. A response with a real JSON body behaves identically — that's asserted by a control, not assumed. The one behaviour change is that an empty 2xx now resolves instead of throwing, which no current endpoint produces.

**Deployment risk:** low. Frontend-only. No API call, no schema, no env var, no dependency, no route. The bundle change is one small function plus three call sites.

**Rollback:** `git revert` the squash commit. Two files, both under `lib/`, nothing persisted, no migration.

**Production verification checklist:**
1. Create a work order — the new row appears and its id is read back (proves real JSON bodies still parse).
2. Edit and save a work order (`apiPut`) — the change persists and no error toast appears.
3. Patch a field inline in a polled table (`apiPatch`) — the value sticks.
4. Trigger a genuine 400, e.g. a CSV import with a bad row — the backend's `detail` still surfaces in the message (`#371` behaviour, which reads the raw error body).
5. Force a 500 on a write and confirm it still reports as a failure, not a silent success.
6. Confirm no new console errors during a normal dashboard poll cycle (`apiGet` unchanged).

author: brianover
body:
Second hero-facing venue, and the owner's *"Do for ALL buildings"* applied to the one that had the least. **Engine suite 889/889, exit 0, clean-tree receipt. Zero `sim/` diff.**

His complaints this answers:

> "why have the interactive things if they just open the same menu lol?"
> "Two mini games both fun but shorter to complete... Do for ALL buildings"

Repo task #70 recorded the tavern as having **zero controls**. Now it has a reason to walk in.

## Act 1 — Work the Room

Every patron card gains a **Pursue** row whenever that hero has a real live thread: an open `Commission` (`TavernPanel.cs:301-305`, reading `state.Commissions`) or an open `OreOffered` (`:308-310`, reading `state.OpenOreOffers`).

Pursuing is **pure local UI selection** — a `_pursued` field, never a `PlayerAction`. Reading the room costs the player nothing; only the handshake commits.

## Act 2 — The Handshake

Renders whatever thread is pursued and commits it through the **exact same actions** `CommissionBoard` and `LedgerModal` already queue: `AcceptCommissionAction`/`DeclineCommissionAction` (Morning-gated) or `BuyOreAction` with a quantity slider (Evening-gated, re-gated live against a tariffed-cost mirror as the slider moves).

A **stale thread** — accepted elsewhere, bought elsewhere, hero died — is re-resolved fresh on every render and shown honestly rather than committed as a lie. Feedback goes through `SimPanel.Confirm` (`:372,381,412`), which already distinguishes an action that resolves on the press from one queued to the bell, so the copy cannot drift from the truth.

## Sim state read, never re-implemented

`GameState.Commissions` and `GameState.OpenOreOffers` (`sim/GameSim/Contracts/World.cs:199,244`), mirroring the phase-legality shape of `ActionLegality.AcceptCommissionLegal`/`DeclineCommissionLegal`/`BuyOreLegal` (`sim/GameSim/Advisor/ActionLegality.cs:606-611,449-492`), and the same tariff formula `LedgerModal.TariffedCost` uses, parametrised for an arbitrary quantity.

## Cut on purpose

**No reflex or precision gauge.** The design (`docs/design/2026-08-04-all-building-minigames.md`) argues the tavern's verbs carry no performance parameter, so a timing layer there would be theatre — busywork dressed as skill. "Shorter" here means fewer steps and less reading, not a minigame.

The bar and corner table are now marked as a cooperating `CombinesWith` pair — the same expression of the owner's "anvil + bellows work together" — while the fireside table keeps its own distinct Eavesdrop route. `StationIdentityTests` still enforces that no two stations share a route unless they are a declared pair.

`MainUi` routing is untouched: all three stations already reach `TavernPanel` with distinct `Copy` toasts, which is exactly what that guard requires.

## One naming note

The section reads "WORK THE ROOM — IN THE COMMON ROOM" on screen, keeping the old substring so the existing `TavernPanelTests` assertions stay meaningful rather than being rewritten to match new copy.

author: aejkatappaja
body:
The Zed theme takes its colours from the palette, but the mapping from a Zed scope to a palette token is written by hand. So a palette change reaches it and a decision in the Neovim groups does not, and a scope Zed emits that the table never names does not degrade to a near miss: Zed resolves a capture to the longest key that is a dotted prefix of it, and falls through to `editor.foreground` when nothing matches, so the text comes out plain.

Read against every `highlights.scm` in `crates/grammars/src` of zed-industries/zed, twelve scopes had no prefix in the table. The syntax table goes from 48 keys to 60.

- `constant.builtin` on sap. Eleven of the twenty-one grammars capture `true`, `false`, `null`, `nil` and every JSON and YAML scalar under it, and it resolved to `constant` on fg, while `boolean` held sap for a capture Zed never emits.
- `namespace`, `module` and `concept` on frost, as `@module` and `@type`.
- `diff.plus`, `diff.minus`, `diff.delta` on ok, error and info, so a diff and a commit stop rendering monochrome.
- `selector` on cinder, which covers the CSS class, id and pseudo scopes through the prefix rule. Selecting an element is what `@tag` does.
- `lifetime` on cinder, where Neovim puts it via `@label`.
- `markup.heading`, `markup.link.url` and `variable.other.member`, all three emitted by the gitcommit grammar.

Four values were wrong rather than absent. `hint` is Zed's inlay hint scope, not its diagnostic one, so it moves from the hint pigment to gutter, where `LspInlayHint` is. `predictive` and `string.doc` drop an italic: `italic_virtual_text` has defaulted to false since #59, and `@string.documentation` was never italic. `emphasis` takes fg and the italic that is the whole definition of `@markup.italic`, instead of an ember it does not have in Neovim.

Bold was missing from the port entirely. `title`, `markup.heading` and `emphasis.strong` go to weight 700. Zed emits `title.markup` for all six heading levels, so the ember-to-fg_dim ladder is not portable and `title` keeps level one.

Three decisions from the groups also never crossed over. The float edge moved to bg5 in #65, so `border` follows it; `pane_group.border` stays on bg3, matching `WinSeparator`, which is why nothing had to be traded. `element.selected` marked the cursor row with the Visual ground, settled on bg2 for that job in #64. That left vis on five keys at once, which hid the last one: a search match was indistinguishable from a selection. It takes brass at 40%, since the key carries no foreground and opaque brass would take the text with it.

The drift check compares a render to itself, so it cannot see an absent scope. The new check implements Zed's prefix resolution and holds twenty-four captures from its own grammars to the palette token their Neovim counterpart takes, plus the weight and the italic. Same shape as the opencode and hunk checks.

Three scopes stay unnamed on purpose. `none` and `text` resolve to `editor.foreground`, which is already the fg Neovim gives them, and `strikethrough.markup` has nothing to bind to: `HighlightStyleContent` cannot express it in v0.2.0.

`extension.toml` stays at 0.1.0. zed-industries/extensions#7032 is still open and nothing is published, so the submodule pin moves and the version does not.

author: arodland
body:
Phone photographs are stored in the sensor's orientation with an EXIF tag (0x0112) saying how to turn them. Neither loader read it.

The consequence is worse than a rotation: `fit_image` computes its cover-crop from the *stored* aspect ratio, so a portrait photo went out as a centre-crop of its own sideways self — which looks like a framing bug rather than a metadata one.

## Approach

Both implementations apply the tag at **open**, before framing.

- **Python** — `sstvae/images.py` gains `open_image`, which is `ImageOps.exif_transpose(Image.open(path))`. Used by `load_image` and by `overlay/render.py` for insets.
- **C++** — `native/third_party/easyexif/` is vendored (BSD, two files, no dependencies) for the JPEG parsing; `images::apply_orientation` does the eight index maps. `images::load` reads the file once and decodes with `stbi_load_from_memory`, since the pixels and the tag come from the same bytes.

Vendoring rather than hand-rolling was the call on the parsing — APP1 segment walking, `II`/`MM` byte order, TIFF IFD offsets and bounds-checking a hostile file are the fiddly half. TinyEXIF was the alternative; easyexif won on its memory-buffer entry point (the shape `load` needs) and on not making tinyxml2 a build-configuration question. Reasoning, including easyexif's dormancy, is recorded in `native/third_party/easyexif/README.md`.

## The divergence this nearly shipped

Pillow honours orientation in a PNG `eXIf` chunk; easyexif parses JPEG only. A tagged PNG would have rotated in Python and not in C++, silently, in the send path. `images.cpp` now locates that chunk and prepends the `Exif\0\0` signature PNG omits, handing the TIFF stream to easyexif — so TIFF parsing stays in the vendored code, and the chunk walk that is ours is a length-prefixed scan with no internal offsets.

That also made the parity comparison **exact**: PNG is lossless, so all eight orientations are compared byte for byte between the implementations. The JPEG comparison cannot be (stb is not libjpeg — an accepted above-the-modem difference), so it instead requires the intended transform to beat all seven alternatives by 4x, which a mere tolerance would not.

## Size limit

Declines any picture file above 1 GiB — before the allocation in C++, before the open in Python. Python raises `ValueError`; `_resolve_source` catches it so an oversized overlay inset draws nothing rather than taking the composition down, and the GUI already surfaces the C++ exception. `MAX_FILE_BYTES` is asserted equal across the two implementations, since nothing derives it and one refusing what the other sends is the failure worth preventing.

## Tests

- `native/tests/test_images.cpp` — 129 checks, new ctest target `images`. The oracle is a second derivation (each orientation as a composition of transpose/mirror-x/mirror-y from the EXIF table), not a restatement of the same inverse maps.
- `tests/test_images_exif.py` — 15, including the framing consequence above.
- `tests/test_native_parity.py` — 16 new, the exact PNG set and the JPEG margin set.

Three mutations verified to fail: swapping the 90° CW/CCW cases (4 checks), dropping `exif_transpose` (all 8 parity cases), stubbing the size comparison (1).

`pytest` 338 passed · `pytest --native` 338 passed · `pytest -m slow` 18 passed, 8 skipped · `ctest` 26/26 · `check_includes` and `check_layering` clean · `images.cpp` cross-compiles under mingw-w64.

## Deliberately not included

`sstvae/data.py`'s training loader and the one-off `scripts/*` that call `Image.open` directly. Rotating training inputs is a change to preprocessing, not to the send path, and shouldn't ride along with this. CLAUDE.md is not amended either.

author: damo1111
body:
## The audit that prompted this

Every road into this app already existed. Every one was behind a trip you hadn't created yet:

| Route | State | Where it lived |
|---|---|---|
| Gmail scan | built and good | only inside an existing trip's planner Overview |
| Forward a booking | built | mentioned once, during onboarding, then never |
| MCP connector | built | URL in Account, under a heading nobody new reads |
| Photos with EXIF | built | could only be added to a trip that already had a name and dates |
| Calendar | **no import at all** | `api/calendar` is a feed *out* |
| Google Timeline | 49 `day_tracks` imported by hand via a script | no UI |

So almost nothing here is new capability. It's the **door**: one sheet listing the ways in, reached from a tile that leads the trip strip and from the empty globe, which now offers "Add a trip you've taken" alongside "Plan a new one".

## Photos, because that's the one genuinely missing

Every other route describes a trip you *booked*. Photos are what you have afterwards, and they carry the two facts that make a trip: when, and roughly where.

`tripFromPhotos.js` does the deciding — 16 tests, no DOM, no network. Photos cluster by a **four-day gap**, chosen to sit between an unphotographed stretch inside one trip and the space between two trips; a pile spanning months comes back as several trips to pick from rather than one impossible fortnight.

**Undated photos are a first-class case, not an error.** WhatsApp, Slack and Google Photos routinely strip EXIF, so they're carried separately and the screen says *"none with a date in them — you'll need to say when"* instead of failing. Nothing is guessed: the title is a month and a year, dates are pre-filled and editable, nothing is written until you press the button. A trip whose last photo is within two days is offered with the end date left open — a trip you're on is the same import.

Dates are read from the first 256KB of each file **before anything uploads**, so the confirm screen can be honest about what it found.

## Measured, not claimed

Through the real pipeline, 24MP source:

| content | original | over the wire | shrink |
|---|---|---|---|
| photographic | 1.66 MB | **86 KB** | 19× |
| pathological noise | 6.43 MB | 879 KB | 7× |

Forty photos is single-digit megabytes rather than 250. The upload screen says what it saved.

## Verification

Browser, 390×844: the tile leads the strip with the demo present; all four routes render; the picker is `multiple` and image-only; an empty globe offers both doors. 152 tests pass, build clean.

## Deliberately not here

- **Google Photos can't be linked.** Google removed broad library read access in 2025; the Picker API that replaced it needs a Cloud project and scope verification. The ordinary file picker reaches Google Photos on Android anyway — which is exactly why undated photos had to work.
- **Google Timeline** stays out until it has a UI. A per-device JSON export isn't a thing to ask of someone on their first run.

author: tishan-harischandra
body:
## What changed

Implements issue #19: the effective-access simulator that answers "why
can this person do this" by running through the real ADS and Cerbos
path for an explicitly named principal - never a client-side or
server-side reimplementation of precedence (§21).

**ADS (the real runtime path, parameterized by an explicit principal):**
- `authz.NewSimulateHandler` serves `POST /internal/authz/simulate`:
  resolves assignments, assembles `permissionContext`, and asks the same
  `PDP`/`Assignments` collaborators the runtime decision endpoint uses,
  labelling the outcome with the same `DecisionSource` function.
- `capability.NewSimulateHandler` serves
  `POST /internal/capabilities/simulate`: reuses `evaluate()` itself -
  the exact target-resolution, leaf-flattening, Cerbos-batching and
  `capabilityeval.Evaluate` composition the runtime capability snapshot
  endpoint uses - with sample attributes supplied directly per
  `targetRef` instead of a resolved real resource.
- `evaluate()` now also returns the full per-leaf outcome map; the
  runtime handler ignores it, the simulate handler uses it to expose the
  complete requirement tree (§12.4) - administration-audience evidence,
  never on an end-user path.
- Both routes are internal-only (reachable only from other backend
  services over the compose network), the same trust boundary every
  other `/internal/*` ADS route already relies on.

**Admin Service:**
- `adsclient` forwards the calling administrator's own bearer token to
  the ADS's internal simulate endpoints - the ADS's own authentication
  middleware verifies it exactly as it would for any other caller, so
  nothing here mints a credential of its own.
- `simulate.Handler` serves `POST /admin/authz/simulate` and
  `POST /admin/authz/simulate-capabilities`, gated by the same
  tenant/hospital authority check every other admin-service write
  endpoint enforces, before forwarding to the ADS.
- `tokenauth.Identity` now carries `RawToken`, mirroring the resource
  service's own identity shape.

**Frontend:** a two-panel Simulator module - one resource-action
simulation with decision source, and a capability simulation showing
every capability's outcome plus the full requirement tree.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] The simulator produces the same answer as the runtime for the
      same inputs, asserted by test - both simulate handlers reuse the
      exact same collaborators (`Assignments`, `PDP`, `DecisionSource`,
      `evaluate()`) the runtime endpoints call, proven directly in
      `apps/ads/internal/authz/simulate_test.go` and

body:
Cappers reported "no NFL lines" on Hall of Fame game night, while prod logs showed the preseason board being fetched and billed: `upcoming americanfootball_nfl_preseason: cost=3`.

Both were true. Books post the whole regular season in August, so the regular-season fetch already returned the full 60-event cap. The merge appended preseason **after** those 60 and sliced back to 60 — discarding every preseason game after paying to fetch it. The survivors were the games furthest away.

Sorting by kickoff before the cap gives the 60 slots to the soonest games. Tonight's Hall of Fame game goes to the top, and in September the regular season reclaims the slots on its own — no seasonal switch to remember.

`sortByKickoff` lives in `odds-board.ts` (the explicit no-`server-only` home for pure board logic) so it is unit-testable.

Regression test asserts the old append-then-cap order **dropped** the Hall of Fame game.

typecheck + 646 tests + build green.

> 
> **Overview**
> Fixes NFL boards showing **no lines** when preseason was fetched but dropped: regular season already filled all **60** slots, preseason was appended and sliced off without reordering.
> 
> **`sortByKickoff`** (in `odds-board.ts`) orders events soonest-first; **`fetchUpcomingOdds`** now dedupes, sorts, then caps so the nearest games keep the slots (August preseason, later regular season). Bad `commenceTime` values sort last.
